name: 13th Age
description: 13th Age is a fantasy tabletop RPG combining classic high- fantasy adventure with innovative storytelling mechanics. Players create heroes in the Dragon Empire setting, forging unique destinies and alliances with powerful Icons (world-shaping NPCs). The game uses a streamlined d20 system with familiar class and level progression, but it forgoes grids for abstract distances to keep combat fast-paced. An Escalation Die mechanic gives players increasing combat advantages each round, and freeform backgrounds replace traditional skill lists to encourage players to weave their characters' backstories directly into gameplay. 13th Age emphasizes collaborative storytelling, allowing the group to co-create setting details and legends through character choices and narrative play.

name: 7th Sea (Second Edition)
description: 7th Sea (Second Edition) is a swashbuckling fantasy role-playing game of high adventure in an alternate 17th-century world. Players take on roles as daring pirates, duelists, musketeers, or explorers in the fictional continent of Théah, which mirrors historical Europe. The game emphasizes cinematic action and dramatic storytelling-players resolve swashbuckling feats by rolling dice pools and creating ""raises"" to accomplish multiple heroic actions at once. The system encourages improvisation and flair, rewarding bold, narrative-driven stunts in both combat and intrigue. Adventures in 7th Sea involve duels at dawn, high-seas voyages, secret societies, and perilous treasure hunts, all capturing the spirit of classic pirate tales and cloak-and-dagger romances.

name: Alien: The Roleplaying Game
description: Alien: The Roleplaying Game is a science- fiction horror RPG set in the universe of the Alien films. Players assume roles such as colonial marines, space truckers, scientists, or androids, all struggling to survive encounters with the deadly Xenomorph and other dangers of space. The game offers two play modes: Cinematic scenarios that emulate the tense, high-fatality one-shot stories of the movies, and Campaign play for longer adventures in the Alien universe. It uses a dice-pool system (roll multiple d6s) where any roll of 6 indicates success. A unique stress mechanic increases a character's dice as they become more frightened (boosting chances to succeed) but also raises the risk of panic if things go wrong. Gameplay emphasizes atmospheric tension, resource management (such as dwindling ammo or air supply), and the constant dread of an unseen terror, faithfully capturing the survival horror feel of the Alien franchise.

name: Avatar Legends: The Roleplaying Game
description: Avatar Legends: The Roleplaying Game is a fantasy RPG set in the world of Avatar: The Last Airbender and The Legend of Korra. Players take on the roles of young heroes-benders who manipulate water, earth, fire, or air, as well as non-bender warriors or technologists- adventuring across the four nations in one of five historical eras of the Avatar universe. Using a narrative-focused Powered by the Apocalypse system, the game emphasizes balance and growth: each character has a playbook (archetype) and 1 must balance between two opposing ideals (such as tradition vs. progress) which guide their character development. Players work together to uphold harmony and confront tyranny or chaos, often facing moral choices reminiscent of the shows. Conflicts are resolved through cinematic descriptions and 2d6-based moves, where success may come with complications. Avatar Legends encourages teamwork, creative use of bending and combat techniques, and role-playing that captures the heart, humor, and heroism of the beloved animated series.

name: Blade Runner: The Roleplaying Game
description: Blade Runner: The Roleplaying Game is a neon-noir sci-fi RPG set in the dystopian future of the Blade Runner universe. Players assume the roles of Blade Runners-special police operatives tasked with hunting down rogue replicants-in the rain-soaked streets of Los Angeles. The game blends investigation, action, and moral ambiguity: players will examine clues, interrogate suspects, and decide how to handle replicants who may be desperate for freedom. Based on a custom adaptation of Free League's Year Zero Engine, mechanics involve rolling pools of six-sided dice for skills, with opportunities for both success and complications (even on the same roll) to generate narrative twists. There are rules for tracking the passage of time and the pressure of cases, as well as a mechanism for the mental stress that comes from the job (including the iconic baseline tests measuring a Blade Runner's emotional stability). The gameplay focuses on casework-each scenario is often a “case file” to be solved-but also downtime and personal dilemmas, forcing characters to grapple with the line between human and artificial life while solving complex cases. With its mix of existential themes and tense set-piece encounters, the Blade Runner RPG delivers the atmosphere of the films: the constant play of light and shadow, and choices that test what it means to be human.

name: Blades in the Dark
description: Blades in the Dark is a gritty, industrial-fantasy role-playing game where players form a crew of scoundrels striving for wealth and power in the haunted city of Doskvol. The setting is reminiscent of a dark Victorian era with magic and steampunk technology: a city of perpetual night, protected from vengeful spirits by lightning barriers. Players choose a crew type (such as Thieves, Assassins, or Smugglers) and undertake daring heists, missions, and schemes to advance their gang's reputation. The system uses a dice-pool of d6s for actions, with outcomes categorized as full success, partial success with complications, or failure (often escalating trouble). It uniquely features a flashback mechanic that allows players to retroactively plan for obstacles during a heist, reducing the need to pre-plan every detail and keeping the game momentum high. A stress mechanic lets characters push themselves for better results or resist negative consequences at the cost of stress (and possibly trauma if overused). Between capers, there's a robust downtime system for characters to recover, train, indulge vices, and expand their crew's influence. Blades in the Dark puts heavy emphasis on emergent narrative and player agency in a sandbox criminal underworld-every decision can shift gang wars, invoke ghostly retributions, or attract the attention of the Bluecoat law. It's a game of bold criminals carving out their legacy amid blood, sweat, and ectoplasm in a city that demands a high price for ambition.

name: Call of Cthulhu
description: Call of Cthulhu is a horror role-playing game of investigation and cosmic dread, inspired by the works of H.P. Lovecraft. Players 2 take on the roles of ordinary people-detectives, professors, journalists, dilettantes, etc.-often in the 1920s (though other time periods are possible) who become drawn into mysterious events and cult conspiracies. The game uses a percentile (d100) skill system: characters have scores in skills like Spot Hidden, Library Use, or Firearms, and must roll under their skill value to succeed in challenges. A defining feature is the Sanity mechanic: as investigators encounter eldritch horrors and forbidden knowledge, they make Sanity checks that can result in temporary or permanent insanity, phobias, and other psychological effects. Combat is deadly and not usually the focus-running away or outsmarting a threat is often wiser than fighting a tentacled abomination head-on. Atmospheric exploration, gathering clues, and solving puzzles or deciphering grim tomes are core activities. Call of Cthulhu gameplay emphasizes tension and the slow realization of the terrible truth, often culminating in desperate attempts to stop a cult ritual or survive an encounter with a Great Old One. Even if characters survive with body intact, their mind might not; the game delivers a poignant sense of horror where victories are often pyrrhic, and the unknown is vast and indifferent.

name: Cyberpunk RED
description: Cyberpunk RED is a futuristic role-playing game that plunges players into the violent, neon-soaked streets of Night City in the mid-2045 era. As a successor to Cyberpunk 2020, it paints a world rebuilding from disaster but still dominated by ruthless megacorporations, augmented gangs, and tangled data networks. Players create edgy characters called edgerunners- such as mercenaries, hackers (Netrunners), tech-experts (Techs), rockers, medtechs, or corporate operatives-each with specific roles and special abilities. The game uses the Interlock system: a d10 + skill + attribute mechanic for actions, where high rolls beat difficulty values. Combat in Cyberpunk RED is tactical, brutal, and often firefight-heavy; it's supported by an array of weapons, cybernetic implants (from neural interfaces to arm blades), and armor that reduce damage. One standout feature is Netrunning: hackers jack into a virtual network called the NET, represented by its own layered “encounter” system of nodes, Black ICE programs, and digital traps, which runs concurrently with real-world action. The style of play encourages creative problem-solving and high-octane action-whether it's a stealthy infiltration of a corporate lab, a street race shootout, or negotiating a deal in a neon club. Characters have the freedom to augment their bodies for performance at the cost of humanity (over-use of cyberware risks cyberpsychosis). Cyberpunk RED immerses players in open-ended missions and dangerous intrigue, capturing the style, attitude, and dystopian themes of classic cyberpunk fiction.

name: Cypher System
description: Cypher System is a flexible, narrative-focused RPG engine designed to run adventures in any genre-fantasy, science fiction, modern thriller, superheroes, you name it. Originally introduced in the game Numenera, the Cypher System uses a streamlined d20-based mechanic that shifts much of the dice-rolling responsibility to the players, while the Game Master mainly sets difficulties. Characters are built using a simple descriptive formula: “I am an [adjective] [noun] who [verbs].” For example, “I am a Quick Explorer who Pilots Starcraft” or “I am a Charming Sorcerer who Wields Fire.” This phrase defines core stats, special abilities, and narrative hooks. There are three core stats (Might, Speed, Intellect) which double as resource pools that players spend to 3 apply Effort (to lower task difficulty) or activate certain powers. To resolve actions, the GM assigns a difficulty level (1–10) and players roll a d20; if the result is equal to or higher than three times the difficulty, it's a success (skills, assets, or spending Effort can lower the difficulty before rolling). Importantly, the GM never rolls dice-NPC actions are always resisted by player rolls-keeping players engaged. The system is also named for “cyphers”: one-use items or bits of tech/magic that characters pick up and expend, encouraging inventive problem-solving and a constantly changing arsenal. Gameplay in the Cypher System is fast and story-driven: instead of micromanaging tactics, players and GMs focus on narrative outcomes, character arcs, and creative uses of abilities. It's a system that encourages improvisation, making it easy to run everything from dungeon crawls to espionage thrillers while maintaining a consistent, easy-to-learn rule framework.

name: Daggerheart
description: Daggerheart is a fantasy role-playing game by Darrington Press (Critical Role's publishing imprint) designed for long-term campaigns and character-driven adventures. It presents a fresh yet familiar take on heroic fantasy: players create characters in a world of magic, monsters, and ancient secrets, embarking on quests that can span an epic saga. The game is built to emphasize both narrative and mechanical depth in equal measure. Players choose classic fantasy roles (warriors, mages, rogues, etc.) but with new twists and progression paths unique to Daggerheart's setting. As characters advance, they gain rich storytelling opportunities-personal quests, relationships, and character arcs are central-alongside increases in power and abilities. Combat in Daggerheart is dynamic and cinematic, using an accessible dice-based system that resolves actions quickly but allows for tactical decisions. (The design philosophy is to keep battles fast-paced and exciting, avoiding slowdowns.) The rules also encourage collaboration between the Game Master and players in world- building and describing action, making each session feel like a cooperative tale. Whether it's delving into a monster-infested ruin, negotiating peace between warring clans, or uniting the land against a looming evil, Daggerheart provides the tools for epic storytelling. It's a game that invites players to get invested in their characters' personal growth as much as the fate of the realm, all while enjoying familiar fantasy gameplay polished by modern design sensibilities.

name: Delta Green
description: Delta Green is a modern horror-espionage role-playing game in which players are secret agents fighting against cosmic horrors and government cover-ups. It evolved from a setting for Call of Cthulhu into a standalone RPG. In Delta Green, the characters are part of an illegal conspiracy (or its government-sanctioned counterpart, depending on era) working within the U.S. government to investigate and neutralize paranormal threats-everything from Lovecraftian entities and alien incursions to cults and unnatural phenomena. The tone is dark, paranoid, and intense: missions are covert, and the public (and often your superiors) can never know the truth. The system is percentile-based (d100) and grounded in realism, reflecting the Call of Cthulhu lineage. Combat with human or unearthly foes is lethal and quick; firearms and explosives do significant damage, and characters don't have action-hero levels of resilience. A key component is the sanity (or willpower) mechanic: witnessing horrors or committing morally terrible acts (even in the line of duty) can erode an agent's 4 mental stability. Delta Green introduces the concept of Bonds (relationships to family, friends, etc.) that agents can tap to reduce stress but at the risk of damaging those relationships-showing how the job can wreck personal lives. During scenarios, players often gather intelligence, conduct surveillance, and piece together clues before deciding on direct action (which might mean a raid, a ritual disruption, or covering up evidence). The game rewards careful planning, ruthless decision-making, and a willingness to sacrifice (others or oneself) for the greater good. Ultimately, Delta Green delivers a chilling experience of fighting horrors both monstrous and conspiratorial, where victory is never clean and often comes at a terrible price.

name: Dungeons & Dragons
description: Dungeons & Dragons is a classic fantasy role-playing game in which players create heroes who band together to explore magical worlds, fight monsters, and find treasure. One participant takes on the role of Dungeon Master (GM), who serves as the storyteller and referee-describing the world and its inhabitants, and presenting challenges for the other players. The players each control a single character, choosing from iconic archetypes like brave fighters, cunning rogues, wise clerics, or spellcasting wizards (among many others). Characters improve by gaining experience points from overcoming obstacles, which leads them to advance in level, becoming more powerful and gaining new abilities. The game's core mechanics involve rolling polyhedral dice to determine the outcomes of risky actions-most notably a twenty-sided die (d20) to resolve attacks, skill checks, and saving throws. For example, when a warrior swings a sword at a dragon, a d20 roll plus modifiers is compared against the dragon's armor to see if the attack hits, and other dice determine the damage. D&D's rules cover a wide range of fantasy adventure elements: combat tactics, spellcasting effects, dungeon hazards, and social interaction. However, the rules are just a framework; much of the gameplay is imaginative and collaborative. Players can attempt anything their characters might plausibly do, and the Dungeon Master adjudicates the results, often facilitating the story in unexpected directions based on player choices. D&D campaigns typically blend action, exploration of fantastic landscapes (like ancient ruins, enchanted forests, or planar realms), and role-playing conversations with NPCs. The game has a flexible setting-it can encompass many worlds and themes from high fantasy epics to gritty medieval adventures. At its heart, Dungeons & Dragons is about a group of friends weaving a heroic tale together, overcoming challenges through strategy, creativity, and teamwork.

name: Dungeon Crawl Classics
description: Dungeon Crawl Classics (DCC) is a fantasy role- playing game that harkens back to the pulp sword-and-sorcery adventures of early RPGs. It emphasizes dungeon exploration, dangerous magic, and high-stakes action in a world filled with strange monsters and arcane secrets. Players often begin with a handful of level-0 characters (peasants and commoners) in a “funnel” adventure, where only the lucky (or clever) survive to become true adventurers. The game uses a modified d20 system but embraces randomness and a wide range of dice (from d3 up to d30) for chaotic, unpredictable outcomes. Combat is straightforward and brutal: a single lucky or unlucky roll can mean a heroic deed or a gruesome death. Spellcasting in DCC is powerful but perilous-each spell can produce wild effects or corrupt the caster if fate is unkind. The system is filled with random tables for critical hits, miscasts, and other 5 events, ensuring that no two sessions are the same. The overall playstyle encourages creativity, risk-taking, and an old-school ethos where cunning and courage matter more than rigid rules. Dungeon Crawl Classics delivers an experience of classic dungeon expeditions and mythical quests, with modern rules twists that keep players on their toes.

name: Dungeon World
description: Dungeon World is a fantasy role-playing game built on the Powered by the Apocalypse system, offering a narrative spin on classic dungeon adventures. Players create traditional adventuring characters-fighters, clerics, thieves, wizards, and more-and undertake quests in a world of monsters and magic. The gameplay focuses on fiction-first storytelling: instead of grid-based tactics, actions are resolved by player moves triggered by the story. Rolling 2d6 plus a relevant ability determines outcomes with tiers of success (10+ full success, 7–9 success with complication, 6 or less the GM reacts with a setback). The rules encourage constant back-and-forth between the GM and players, with the GM following principles and making “soft” and “hard” moves in response to player actions. Dungeon World retains the feel of exploring dungeons, fighting monsters, and earning treasure, but with an emphasis on improvisation, player input into the world, and cinematic descriptions over meticulous mechanics. It's a gateway to the old-school adventure vibe through modern, streamlined play.

name: Dragonbane
description: Dragonbane is a fantasy role-playing game by Free League Publishing, serving as a modern reimagining of Sweden's classic Drakar och Demoner. It offers a classic fantasy adventure experience filled with “mirth and mayhem” - a mix of epic quests and lighthearted tone. Players create heroes (such as brave knights, rogues, dwarves, or sorcerers) and explore a richly detailed world of dragons, magic, and heroic deeds. The system uses a fast roll- under d20 mechanic with “boons” and “banes” (advantage/disadvantage-style modifiers) that make combat and action resolution quick and swingy. Characters have heroic abilities that let them perform extraordinary feats, and combat is lively and often unpredictable, encouraging cinematic play. Dragonbane is designed to accommodate both one-shot dungeon crawls and long-term campaigns, emphasizing fun, accessible play while channeling the spirit of classic fantasy role-playing.

name: Dune: Adventures in the Imperium
description: Dune: Adventures in the Imperium is a tabletop RPG that transports players to the renowned universe of Frank Herbert's Dune, where political intrigue, noble houses, and deadly conflict unfold on an interstellar stage. In this game, the players typically serve as key agents of a noble House (Atreides, Harkonnen, or a new House of their creation), navigating the deadly politics, espionage, and warfare of the Imperium. Adventures often involve diplomacy and deception one moment and knife-fights or ornithopter chases the next. The system uses Modiphius's 2d20 ruleset, which encourages cinematic and narrative-driven action. Players roll two (or more) twenty-sided dice against a target number (derived from attributes + skills) and count each die that rolls under the number as a success; extra successes generate Momentum that can be spent for added benefits. Meanwhile, the GM can use Threat (a pool gained from player actions or difficult circumstances) to introduce complications or escalate dangers. Unique to Dune are mechanics for architect- level play (influencing large-scale strategies and House assets) and for duels and conflicts of both words and weapons. Characters have Drives (like Duty, 6 Faith, or Power) representing core motivations, which can influence their rolls and decisions. The gameplay emphasizes making hard choices in line with one's principles or ambitions-choosing between love or duty, survival or honor. The tone is thoughtful and intense: every encounter could be a test of loyalty or a trap set by an enemy. With its focus on high stakes and complex human drama, Dune: Adventures in the Imperium captures the spirit of the novels, allowing players to scheme, fight, and sacrifice as part of a grand saga of empire.

name: Fate Core System
description: Fate Core System is a flexible, narrative-driven tabletop RPG framework designed to work with any setting or genre. Instead of focusing on detailed simulations, Fate emphasizes storytelling and character traits known as Aspects-short phrases that describe something important about a character or situation (e.g., “Sharp-Eyed Archer” or “Never Leaves a Friend Behind”). Players can invoke their Aspects by spending Fate points to gain bonuses or narrative advantages, and the GM can compel Aspects to introduce complications that drive the story. The mechanics use Fate dice (six-sided dice with sides marked +, -, or blank) to determine outcomes: you roll four Fate dice and add a skill level, with pluses adding and minuses subtracting. The resulting total is compared against a difficulty; shifts above or below determine success, failure, or succeeding at a cost. Characters are further defined by skills (broad competencies like Fight, Stealth, Diplomacy) and stunts (special abilities that provide a perk or a rule-breaking benefit in certain situations). Fate Core encourages collaborative world-building: during game creation, players and the GM work together to establish setting Aspects (like “City of Spires in Civil War” or “Magic is Dying”) that affect everyone. Conflict-whether a fencing duel, a debate, or a car chase-is handled with the same core mechanics, often extended into a contest or combat with zones and exchanges, but always keeping the focus on the narrative purpose of actions (“I swing from the chandelier to kick the sword from his hand” rather than “I move 30 feet and make one melee attack”). The system is light on modifiers and stats, instead rewarding creativity: almost any situation can be improved by creating an Advantage (adding a new Aspect to a scene, like “Distracted by the Alarum” for guards if you set off a noise). Fate's design makes it easy to improvise and adapt; the GM is encouraged to say “yes, but…” or “yes, and…” to player ideas, using Aspects and Fate points to keep things balanced. In essence, Fate Core System provides a toolkit for telling dynamic, character-focused stories where the rules have your back but never get in the way of the narrative you want to create.

name: Forbidden Lands
description: Forbidden Lands is a dark fantasy role-playing game that blends old-school survival adventure with modern mechanics. Players take on the roles of rogues and raiders-adventurers who are not necessarily noble heroes but survivors and opportunists-in a cursed realm known as the Forbidden Lands. This world was sealed off by a Blood Mist for generations, which only recently lifted, allowing expeditions into its long-isolated territories filled with ruins, monsters, and long-lost treasures. The game uses the Year Zero Engine (a pool of d6s) with a push-your-roll mechanic: you assemble dice for attribute, skill, and gear, roll for 6s as successes, and you may reroll failures at the risk of taking damage or exhaustion if 1s come up on certain dice. Survival elements are key: players must manage food, water, and sleep, and navigation is done on a hex map where each journey can bring random encounters or hazards. The 7 system features a robust exploration and camp-building aspect-players can establish a stronghold over time, which grants benefits and a sense of home in the dangerous wilds. Combat is fast and gritty: critical injuries can maim or kill, and even a skilled fighter can fall to a lucky goblin ambush if fate frowns. Magic is present but often subtle or costly, fitting the low-magic atmosphere. What sets Forbidden Lands apart is its open-world, sandbox approach: the GM presents a world filled with legends and locations (detailed in treasure and adventure site modules), but the players decide where to go and which rumors to follow. The tone is harsh yet adventurous: the world's history is rich with war and sorcery, and while the people have suffered under darkness, now is the time when bold outlaws can carve their names in saga-if the curses of the past or the claws of a death wyrm don't claim them first.

name: GURPS (Generic Universal Role-Playing System)
description: GURPS (Generic Universal Role-Playing System) is a flexible tabletop RPG system designed to simulate any setting or genre imaginable. Instead of classes or levels, GURPS uses a point- buy character creation: players allocate points to buy attributes (like Strength, Intelligence), skills (from Swordsmanship to Computer Hacking), advantages (special talents or powers, like Night Vision or Wealth), and disadvantages (flaws like Bad Temper or a Phobia, which give extra points to spend). This results in highly customized characters built to fit the exact concept desired, whether that's a cyberpunk detective with a robotic arm, a vampire aristocrat, or a vanilla medieval blacksmith turned reluctant adventurer. The core mechanic uses six-sided dice: typically roll 3d6 and try to get under a target number (usually a skill or attribute) to succeed, with the margin indicating the degree of success or failure. The system is renowned for its consistency and emphasis on realism: measurements, time, and effects are scaled to real-world physics where appropriate, and there are optional rules for everything from running out of ammo to the trauma from injuries. Combat in GURPS can be as straightforward or detailed as desired-at base, it's an exchange of attack and defense rolls (roll under skill to hit, opponent rolls under defense to dodge or parry). But with advanced rules, one can include hit locations, different maneuver options (all-out attack, defensive stance), facing and posture, etc., making it a tactical simulation if players want that. One hallmark is how GURPS handles damage: instead of inflating hit points with level, damage is directly subtracted from a character's small pool of hit points (often around 10-12 for a human). A solid weapon hit can incapacitate or kill a person quickly, so combat tends to be dangerous and strategic. Magic, superpowers, and other fantastic abilities are constructed through GURPS's advantage system: for example, a fireball spell might be built as an Innate Attack advantage with the Burning damage modifier and a mana-based limitation. GURPS has extensive sourcebooks covering specific genres (GURPS Fantasy, GURPS Space), settings (GURPS Middle Ages, GURPS Mars), and even particular IPs. The system is modular: groups pick which rules and options fit their game, making it scalable from light cinematic action (ignoring realism and complexity) to heavy simulationist play (tracking encumbrance, recoil, etc.). Because of this, GURPS can handle a campaign that starts as pulp adventure, turns into interstellar exploration, and ends with psychic duelists, all with consistent underlying rules. The result is a game of incredible freedom, where anything not explicitly 8 listed can be improvised using the existing mechanics. GURPS appeals to those who want a unified system for all their games or love fine-tuning every aspect of a character or world with mechanical representation. It's often praised for its balance and logical design, enabling players to attempt wild ideas in play and GMs to adjudicate them using a solid framework. In essence, GURPS provides the tools to build your own RPG reality, whether mirroring our own or creating one that's never been seen before.

name: King Arthur Pendragon
description: King Arthur Pendragon is a role-playing game that lets players experience the epic legends of King Arthur and his knights, focusing on the ideals of chivalry, romance, and the rise and fall of Camelot. Each player typically takes the role of a knight of the Round Table era (or their own knightly ancestor as years pass), and the campaign spans decades of game time, following the arc of Arthurian legend from the early struggles to the golden age and ultimately to the tragedy of the fall. Pendragon uniquely centers the game on the feudal and moral landscape of Arthurian Britain: characters have attributes but also a set of paired Traits (like Valorous vs. Cowardly, Generous vs. Selfish) that quantify their personality and tendencies, as well as Passions (like Loyalty to Lord, Love (Family), Honor, Hatred of Saxons, etc.) that can inspire them to great deeds or drive them into reckless actions. The game uses a d20 roll-under system: to succeed at a skill or weapon roll, you must roll equal or under your skill value on d20 (rolling exactly your skill is a critical success). In opposed checks (like two knights jousting), the higher successful roll wins, making combat a deadly comparison of skill and luck. Damage is rolled on many d6s (a strong knight on a charging warhorse can roll a dozen or more d6 damage), and can outright knock a knight unconscious or kill them if it's high enough compared to their armor. The winter phase each year allows knights to heal, manage their estate, attempt to advance their standing (through marriage or training), and have children. Thus, lineage becomes important: as the years go by, player knights age, may die of battle or illness, and their children take up the mantle-allowing the saga to continue across generations. The ultimate goal is often Glory: the game quantifies a knight's renown, and much of play is about pursuing glorious deeds (slaying a mighty beast, leading a battle, upholding a knightly virtue even when it's hard) to increase that Glory and earn a place in history. Magic and the supernatural exist but are mostly subtle or tied to creatures like the fey; player knights are generally not casting spells (unless someone plays a sorcerer which is a very different kind of campaign). This keeps the focus on martial and moral challenges. The default setting follows the literary timeline of Arthur-starting with Uther's reign, the anarchy after his death, Arthur's rise (where the players might help him draw the sword or fight at his side to unify Britain), the high glory years of chivalric romance, and then the slow descent as personal failings and external treachery (the affair of Lancelot and Guinevere, Mordred's rebellion) tear everything down. Playing Pendragon feels like living through a great novel of knighthood: one moment you're in a grand tournament showing off courtly skills, another you're grimly holding a frontier against raiding Saxons, and later you might quest for the Holy Grail or govern a dukedom. Throughout, the game emphasizes being a knight-the code of conduct, the weight of expectations, and the poignant balance between pursuing personal desires (love, vengeance, ambition) and 9 fulfilling duties (to one's lord, family, and ideals). It's an immersive experience that stands apart from most RPGs in its scope and thematic focus, truly aiming to make players feel they are part of an enduring Arthurian legend.

name: Legend of the Five Rings Roleplaying Game
description: Legend of the Five Rings (L5R) Roleplaying Game is set in the fictional land of Rokugan, a feudal Asian- inspired world where honor is life and samurai of Great Clans serve their Emperor. Players become samurai of Rokugan - who could be bushi (warriors), courtiers (diplomats), shugenja (priests wielding elemental magic), or monks - from one of the Great Clans (Crab, Crane, Dragon, Lion, Phoenix, Scorpion, Unicorn, plus others like Minor Clans) each with distinct philosophies and styles. The game strongly focuses on social etiquette, duty, and the conflicts that arise between personal feelings and societal obligations. The Roll & Keep game system in earlier editions had players roll a pool of d10s (based on trait + skill), keep a number of them (based on trait), and sum them, looking to exceed a target number. The latest edition by Fantasy Flight Games uses custom dice with symbols and a narrative approach, emphasizing Strife (emotional turmoil) and choosing how far to push yourself. In any edition, combat can be swift and deadly - a katana strike or well-placed arrow can kill or incapacitate quickly, so duels are often high-stakes and brief. Much of the game involves intrigue and decision-making: one might be negotiating peace at court one session and investigating a spirit disturbance in a village the next. A unique aspect of L5R is its emphasis on Honor, Glory, and Status as mechanical values that influence how a character should act and how they are perceived. Characters also have deeply held personal and clan-oriented beliefs, and violating those (or facing temptations like treachery or love) provides rich roleplaying moments. Magic in Rokugan is divine in nature: shugenja invoke elemental kami to create effects, whether calling flames or requesting rains. The supernatural exists in the form of demons (oni), spirits, fortunes (gods), and the taint of Fu Leng (a corrupting evil force) - facing these is part of a samurai's duty, often at great peril. Ultimately, Legend of the Five Rings is about living (and often dying) by a code in a world where the right choice isn't always clear. Players must balance their loyalty to their lord, their clan, the Emperor, and their own personal sense of what is just. A single stroke of a sword or a single misspoken word in court can turn the tide of their fortunes. This creates a dramatic, tension-filled experience where heroism is measured as much by one's integrity and resolve as by martial prowess.

name: Marvel Multiverse Role-Playing Game
description: Marvel Multiverse Role-Playing Game is a superhero RPG that lets players step into the roles of iconic Marvel superheroes or create their own original heroes in the Marvel Comics universe. It features familiar characters, locations, and villains from the expansive lore -from Avengers and X-Men to cosmic beings. The game uses the custom “d616” dice system, a nod to Marvel's primary Earth-616 continuity: players roll three six- sided dice (with one die designated as the “Marvel die”), and add ability modifiers to beat a target number for actions. Rolling a 6-1-6 (in any order) is a Fantastic roll, often granting extraordinary success or bonus effects. Characters are defined by their hero archetype and power sets; for instance, a Blaster might excel in ranged attacks (like Iron Man's repulsors), while a 10 Striker focuses on melee (like Wolverine). Powers are listed in ranks and have specific in-game effects, but there's flexibility to flavor them to match the hero (energy blasts, weather control, super strength, etc.). The system emphasizes fast-paced, cinematic action: heroes can team up for combos, use “karma” (a metacurrency) to influence rolls or alter scenes, and pull off stunts in line with comic book logic. In combat, characters have a set of actions (movement, attack, etc.) and the focus is on dynamic descriptions-smashing through walls, bouncing shields off enemies, using the environment. Outside of fights, the game covers things like social interactions and problem-solving with a straightforward skill system tied to the dice mechanic (d616 plus relevant stat). The tone is four-color Marvel fun: while death and darkness can occur, the game largely encourages heroics and optimistic problem-solving. Campaigns might involve stopping a bank robbery one session and thwarting Thanos the next, scaling according to the heroes' power levels. By default, it provides stat blocks for dozens of famous heroes and villains, allowing groups to jump in and play out “what-if” scenarios or reenact classic storylines. The Marvel Multiverse RPG encapsulates the feel of Marvel comics: high-energy, dramatic, and full of teamwork, where every hero's turn can be a splash-page moment. Whether you're swinging through New York as Spider-Man, bantering while blasting bad guys as Star-Lord, or unleashing cosmic power as Captain Marvel, the game aims to deliver the thrill of being a Marvel superhero.

name: Monster of the Week
description: Monster of the Week is a modern horror/adventure role-playing game in which players become intrepid monster hunters facing supernatural threats. Inspired by TV shows like Buffy the Vampire Slayer, Supernatural, and The X-Files, the game is structured around episodic mysteries where each session (or story arc) features a new monster and a strange phenomenon to investigate. Players choose from archetypal playbooks like the Chosen (destined hero), the Expert (knowledgeable scholar), the Spooky (has innate psychic or dark powers), the Mundane (ordinary person who ends up in extraordinary situations), and more - each with unique moves and traits that contribute to the team. Using the Powered by the Apocalypse system, the mechanics are narrative-focused: players roll 2d6 plus a relevant stat (like Tough, Cool, Sharp, Charm, Weird) when they trigger moves such as “kick some ass” (combat), “investigate a mystery,” or “manipulate someone.” On a 10+ they succeed well, on a 7–9 they succeed with a complication or hard choice, and on a 6 or less the situation escalates (and the Master of Ceremonies, i.e., GM, gets to introduce a twist or danger). Combat is quick and always two-sided - when you fight a monster, it often can hurt you back, so hunters must be smart about preparation, using weaknesses, and teamwork. A big part of the game is the investigative phase: asking the right questions to figure out the monster's weaknesses and motives, and gathering the tools or allies needed to face it. Every monster has specific conditions to defeat it - just staking a vampire or getting a ghost's bones buried properly, for example - so engaging with the story is key; it's not just about blasting everything with guns (though you can try). Characters have limited Luck points they can burn to avoid damage or guarantee success, but Luck is precious, as running out marks the hunter for impending doom narratively. Monster of the Week encourages collaborative creation of the setting (often a town or region with recurring locations and 11 NPCs) and a relatively light tone mixed with genuine creepiness. The group usually forms a team (the game assumes a shared drive to hunt monsters) and could range from a ragtag group of civilians thrown together to a formal agency task force. The charm of the game is in its embrace of monster-hunting tropes: researching in dusty libraries, bantering during stakeouts, dramatic confrontations in spooky locations, and the emotional toll on hunters leading dangerous double-lives. In the end, each mystery is resolved by confronting the monster of the week in a climactic showdown, ideally having deduced its vulnerability and set a trap or plan into motion. After the smoke clears, the hunters live to fight another day - and maybe grab a slice of pie at the diner while nursing their wounds, wondering where the next case will take them.

name: Mörk Borg
description: Mörk Borg is a rules-light fantasy role-playing game known for its grimdark, heavy-metal aesthetic and doom-laden tone. Set in a decaying, dying world, players take on the roles of desperate anti-heroes, scoundrels, and outcasts facing a relentless apocalypse prophesied through miseries and blasphemies. The game's art and writing evoke a punk sensibility: pages splattered with neon ink and gothic imagery, text that howls with nihilism and dark humor. Characters are fragile and expendable - classes (if used) include things like Gutterborn Scum or Fanged Deserter, each with minimal starting gear and bizarre traits (like a mechanically useless but flavorful “omnious presence” or a spinal growth). The mechanics use a simple d20 roll-under system for actions: players roll a d20, add or subtract a small attribute modifier, and compare to a difficulty or opponent; combat uses this same roll for attacks (trying to meet or beat an enemy defense) and defense (enemies don't roll to hit; players roll to avoid being hit). Damage is by weapon type (often a d6 or d4) minus any armor's damage reduction. With low hit points (typically 1d8 or similar), death is always a hit or two away. Healing is scarce, and critical hits or fumbles can maim or corrupt. A distinctive feature is the calendar of misery: the world is ending, and the GM is prompted to roll for apocalyptic events (like the sun fading or the earth opening) at certain intervals; after a certain number of such miseries, the game world is destroyed in an inevitable cataclysm. This creates urgency - it's understood that everything in Mörk Borg is fleeting. Magic exists via scrolls but is unpredictable and potentially catastrophic (miscasting a scroll can have effects like summoning something awful or deforming the caster). The game actively encourages creativity and randomness: there are many tables for things like horrible findings in a corpse's pockets or occult treasures, but few hard-coded “campaign” details beyond a general sense of a dying land and a cruel monarch. The tone balances on the edge of bleak and absurd: it's horrifying that you might be disemboweled by a demon, but the game presents it with a wink and a thrasher's grin, perhaps accompanied by a one-liner or a comically excessive description. Mörk Borg sessions often involve survival-style dungeon crawls or journeys through plague- ridden landscapes, where the goal might simply be to grab loot and get out alive before something awful happens. There is little promise of happy endings or heroism - more often, player characters might end up causing as much chaos as they prevent. In summary, Mörk Borg is an experience - a fusion of art-punk design and minimalist play - where every swing of the axe and cast of a die courts death or dismemberment, and the only reward is living to see the sun 12 (barely) rise on another miserable day. It's a love letter to the darker side of fantasy, perfect for one-shots or short campaigns where mood and mayhem take center stage.

name: Mutant: Year Zero
description: Mutant: Year Zero is a post-apocalyptic role-playing game in which players portray mutants surviving in the ruins of civilization. The world has been devastated by some unspecified apocalypse (disease, war, and environmental collapse all rolled together), and the only haven for the player characters is the Ark - a small, isolated mutant community. All the player characters (and everyone in the Ark) are mutants, who are generally infertile and in their teens or early adulthood; there have been no new children, adding an overarching desperation to their society. The game loop alternates between tending to the Ark (developing it and dealing with its political struggles) and going on expeditions into the Zone (the dangerous wasteland beyond the Ark) to scavenge resources and knowledge. The system uses the Year Zero Engine: players have pools of six-sided dice for actions based on attribute + skill + gear. Rolling 6s means success, 1s on certain dice can mean trouble. If a roll fails, a player can choose to “push” - reroll all dice that weren't 6s, but any 1s showing then will inflict stress or damage (to attributes or gear). This creates a push-your-luck tension fitting for a desperate world. Each character has a mutation (like telepathy, flame breath, or reptilian regeneration) which can give a powerful edge, but mutants must spend Mutation Points to use them (often gained by pushing rolls), and some mutation outcomes can be unpredictable or taxing. Life in the Ark is a big part of MYZ: at the start, the Ark is in bad shape (no reliable food source, no decent shelter, etc.). The group collectively chooses “projects” to improve it (like starting farms, building walls, or restoring a generator), which require certain artifacts or successes to complete. How the Ark grows (tracked with Development Levels in things like Food, Culture, Technology, Warfare) affects what later challenges or advantages they have. NPC “bosses” and “gangs” in the Ark jostle for power, and the players can align or clash with them. Venturing into the Zone is dangerous: the landscape is dotted with “Zone sectors” that might contain abandoned bunkers, wreckage, or weird phenomenon, often with some threat (zone monsters, environmental hazards, or active ancient security systems). The Zone is also contaminated, and characters risk accumulating rot (a radiation-like illness) the longer they stay out. The ultimate carrot in Mutant: Year Zero is the potential of finding Eden - a legendary safe haven that may hold the answers to the mutants' origins and the key to their future. Clues about Eden can be among the artifacts they find. This search gives a sense of direction to exploration. Tone-wise, Mutant: Year Zero is gritty and survivalist (scrounging bullets and grub is a constant concern) but also plucky and hopeful in a way - the characters, despite being misfits and sometimes physically odd, form a tight “PC crew” (like a found family) with unique Roles like the Boss, Gearhead, Stalker, Chronicler etc., complementing each other. There's often a gallows humor at the strangeness they encounter (like a deranged robot still tending a crumbling amusement park, or a giant zone pig that's made a lair in an old supermarket). As the campaign progresses, they might evolve from scrappy scavengers to leaders of their people, guiding the Ark toward a better future (or tearing it apart if things go wrong). In essence, Mutant: Year Zero delivers a blend of exploration, 13 community-building, and X-Men-like flair (because of the mutations), all wrapped in a harsh sandbox world that players get to gradually tame - or at least understand - one derelict sector at a time.

name: Mutants & Masterminds
description: Mutants & Masterminds (Third Edition) is a superhero role-playing game that allows players to create virtually any comic- book style hero or villain imaginable. It uses a d20-based system heavily modified for point-buy character creation and scaling of superpowers. Instead of classes or levels (though characters do have a Power Level that serves as a balance benchmark), players spend power points to build their hero's attributes, skills, advantages (small perks or combat feats), and especially powers. Powers are constructed with effects (damage, flight, illusion, mind control, etc.) and then modified with descriptors and extras or flaws (like making an attack Area effect, or limiting a power to only work in sunlight). This means one hero's “blast” might be eye lasers and another's might be magical fire, but mechanically they can be built using the same effect with different descriptors. The system resolves actions with a d20 roll plus modifiers against a difficulty (similar to D&D's d20 core). However, there are no traditional hit points. Instead, if you're hit by an attack, you make a Toughness saving throw (d20 + Toughness vs. DC set by attack's damage). If you fail by some margin, you accumulate conditions (dazed, impaired, etc.) or take a “Bruise” (which gives a penalty on further Toughness checks), and failing significantly can knock you out (or even kill, if the campaign allows lethal stakes). This makes combat cinematic: you're often fine until that one big hit or a piling on of penalties takes you down. Other defenses (Dodge, Will, etc.) protect against different attack types and have their own checks. M&M places a big emphasis on dynamic action and player creativity: players can use Hero Points (a resource earned for things like roleplaying disadvantages or suffering setbacks) to reroll bad results or enact stunts (power stunts let you temporarily use your powers in a new way, e.g., a fire hero making a blazing wall for one scene). The game supports everything from street-level vigilantes to cosmic powerhouses by adjusting Power Level and point totals. Power Level imposes caps to ensure balance (e.g., at PL 10, an attack bonus + damage rank typically shouldn't exceed 20 combined, so you could be very accurate but lower damage or vice versa). This keeps heroes in a similar effectiveness range even with very different builds. Characters also have complications - personal issues or motivations (like a secret identity, a loved one frequently in peril, or a temper) that the GM can invoke to add drama, awarding Hero Points when they cause trouble. Because of its modular nature, M&M can emulate many comic styles: you could run a gritty street gang game like The Defenders or a high-flying Justice League or Avengers style game. Adventures might involve classic comic scenarios: stopping a bank robbery, foiling a villain's world domination scheme, rescuing citizens from a natural disaster, navigating an alternate dimension, or teaming up to battle a villainous super-team. The focus is on the larger-than- life heroics: the rules encourage descriptors and flair (just doing a “Strength check” is described as ripping open the steel door or holding back the collapsing bridge, etc.). In summation, Mutants & Masterminds provides a crunchy yet flexible framework to live out superhero fantasies, where players can truly customize their heroes' powers and the narrative emphasizes heroic deeds, clever 14 problem-solving, and the occasional dramatic twist of fate that tests their characters' resolve and ideals.

name: Numenera
description: Numenera is a far-future science-fantasy role-playing game set on Earth one billion years from now in the Ninth World. Countless civilizations have risen and fallen in that time, leaving behind a landscape littered with the remnants of their ultra-advanced technologies - these devices and biotech artifacts are collectively known as “numenera,” and though they appear magical to the current inhabitants, they are actually relics of science. Players take on the roles of explorers and adventurers seeking to understand and utilize these numenera for the betterment of their people or personal gain. Character creation follows a simple yet flavorful formula: each character is described by a sentence “I am an [adjective] [noun] who [verbs].” The noun is the Type (Glaive- warrior, Nano-tech/magic user, or Jack-jack-of-all-trades), the adjective is a Descriptor (like Charming, Stealthy, or Rugged, which adds unique bonuses and quirks), and the verb phrase is a Focus - a unique specialization such as “Controls Gravity,” “Rides the Lightning,” or “Bears a Halo of Fire,” which gives a suite of themed abilities. This defines most of the character's capabilities and suggests background and personality. Numenera uses the Cypher System rules: tasks have difficulties rated 1 to 10. To succeed, a player must roll equal or above the difficulty multiplied by 3 on a d20 (so difficulty 4 means target number 12). Characters can lower the difficulty by applying skills, using assets (tools or help), or spending effort (which costs points from their stat pools-Might, Speed, or Intellect). Importantly, players roll all dice; when a monster attacks, the player rolls defense. A roll of 1 can trigger a GM intrusion (a complication, often yielding XP to players as compensation), and a roll of 19 or 20 can grant minor or major bonuses. There are no traditional classes or levels; advancement grants increased stats or new abilities chosen from those available to your Type or Focus. A distinctive element is the Cyphers - one-use numenera items that characters frequently discover. These might be grenades, odd healing devices, teleportation pods, or truly weird biotech injections that do something wondrous. Cyphers encourage creative problem- solving and a constantly changing arsenal; players are expected to use them freely (and the GM awards new ones often). The Ninth World setting of Numenera is intentionally mysterious and awe-inspiring. The game's ethos is “discovery” - encountering strange devices, creatures, and phenomena and figuring out what they are or how to use them. One adventure might involve negotiating peace between villages with the aid of a floating ancient automaton they worship as a god, and the next might be delving into a crashed hovering city to retrieve a solar-powered numenera that can save the crops. The tone blends optimism and wonder with survival and superstition; societies are generally medieval in level (with city-states, petty kingdoms, and limited knowledge of the world) but everywhere are colossal ruins, mechanical creatures, and unexplained wonders from prior epochs. For example, the Iron Wind is a freakish nano-tech storm that disassembles and reshapes anything in its path; the Beanstalk is a massive pillar reaching into orbit that locals see as a giant tree. As players adventure, they often piece together bits of ancient knowledge, but the game emphasizes that the “truth” may be less important than how you use the numenera in front of you. Numenera offers a unique mix of simple mechanics empowering a 15 free-flowing narrative, characters who feel competent and customizable, and an endlessly imaginative world that sparks curiosity. It asks: what do you do with the power and knowledge of a billion years past, and can you use it to build a better future - or at least make it to tomorrow's adventure?

name: Old School Essentials
description: Old School Essentials (OSE) is a tabletop RPG that faithfully revives and refines the classic Basic/Expert Dungeons & Dragons rules from the early 1980s for modern play. It captures the old-school feel of dungeon crawls and sandbox exploration with an emphasis on rulings over rules and player ingenuity. Characters are created within straightforward classes like Fighter, Cleric, Thief, Wizard (and demihumans as classes, e.g., Dwarf, Elf, Halfling, each combining race and profession). Ability scores modify rolls, but they are not as dominant as in later editions; player decisions and creativity often matter more than high stats. The core mechanics are simple: most task resolutions or saving throws require rolling a d20 and aiming to get equal or above a target number (for attacks, that target is the opponent's AC; for saves, it's a fixed number on your class table). Armor Class can be played as descending (old school style, where lower is better) or ascending (modern style) as OSE provides both options for ease. Damage is determined by weapon type (with most melee weapons dealing around 1d6 by the book) and hit points are low, especially at first level, which makes every encounter potentially deadly. The game strongly encourages mapping and resource management: torches, rations, encumbrance, time tracking for exploration turns, etc., to build tension and make dungeon delves a logistical challenge. Magic is Vancian for wizards and clerics (memorize spells, expend them when cast), and spells have concise descriptions often open to clever interpretation (sleep spell can upend a low- level encounter, but then you have to figure out what to do with the snoozing monsters!). OSE's presentation is a hallmark: it reorganizes those classic rules with clean layout and clear language, making a game that was sometimes seen as obtuse into something very accessible. The tone of play is emergent fantasy adventure - there isn't an epic plot baked in, but rather the players create the story through actions in a world the Game Master presents. Often it's about venturing into monster-filled ruins, outwitting traps, discovering weird magic items (like a bag of devouring or boots of levitation), and hauling treasure back to town - where experience points are mainly gained from treasure spent, reinforcing the treasure-seeking motive. Characters in OSE advance relatively quickly at low levels but the power curve is flatter than modern games; high- level play still sees fighters with at most maybe 9 attacks (versus a horde of goblins) and wizards with potent spells but limited slots, rather than godlike powers. And death is always a missed saving throw away (poison might kill you outright, falling rocks too). Yet this risk creates excitement and creative play: players tend to think outside the box, ask lots of questions, and come up with plans to avoid fair fights, because charging in isn't always a viable option. Old School Essentials supports classic modules and homebrew easily; it basically is B/X D&D polished, so decades of content are at your disposal. In summary, Old School Essentials delivers a fast, flavorful fantasy RPG experience where the rules are light but solid, the adventuring world is dangerous and full of wonder, and the story emerges from how players tackle the challenges presented - often in delightfully unorthodox ways." 16

name: Paranoia
description: Paranoia is a darkly comedic science fiction RPG set in the dystopian underground city of Alpha Complex, which is controlled by The Computer - a cheerful but deranged AI. Players are cast as Troubleshooters, citizens of Alpha Complex who have been granted the (often fatal) privilege of hunting down threats to society, like traitors and mutants. The twist is that every player character *is* a traitor of some sort: each belongs to a secret society (from Commies to Psionics to Rebels) and likely has a hidden mutant power, all of which are illegal under The Computer's regime. Gameplay is oriented around missions given by The Computer (via terse, absurd briefings) that are invariably ill-defined, physically hazardous, and rife with opportunities for blame. The rules encourage a very fast, backstabbing-oriented play style. Players have six clones (lives) because they will die - often - from accidents, laser battles, “friendly fire,” or summary execution for treason. The Computer is omnipresent via cameras and expects strict adherence to its illogical rules (“Happiness is mandatory” is a classic). The humor arises as players attempt to complete tasks while hiding their own treasonous behaviors and uncovering (or fabricating) those of their teammates. For example, one Troubleshooter might receive a secret objective to ensure another doesn't return from the mission alive. Official rules infractions (like seeing the wrong color clearance area or failing to file paperwork) can be used as excuses to eliminate rivals. The system (varies by edition) is usually fairly simple - combat often resolved by laser shots and explosions, with little worry for realism. Equipment given to Troubleshooters usually includes experimental gadgets that malfunction spectacularly. Paranoia's narrative is fast-paced and encourages the Game Master (called “The Computer” or “GM”) to be arbitrary and capricious. Player success is less about character build (which is generally basic) and more about clever improv, paranoia (the feeling), and sometimes just luck. Missions might involve things like repairing a food vat (that is full of mutant alligators) or testing a new weapon (that is more dangerous to the user than the target). After each mission, surviving Troubleshooters often have debriefings where they shift blame to their dead teammates. Paranoia is unique in that it's often adversarial among players by design - though all in service of humor and an over-the-top experience. The ideal Paranoia session leaves everyone laughing at the ridiculous lengths the characters go to please The Computer or eliminate each other. Trust is non- existent; everyone is out to get ahead, survive, or hide their own secrets under the guise of smiling loyalty. In short, Paranoia is a game where you might be ordered to scrub a corridor with a toothbrush, while your teammate is secretly trying to dose you with a slow-acting poison, and your equipment is actively trying to explode, and if you complain, The Computer might vaporize you for lack of enthusiasm - and that's a normal day in Alpha Complex. It's gleefully cruel, chaotically fun, and unlike any other RPG in the way it encourages you to undermine your friends (in character) and revel in the absurdity.

name: Pathfinder Roleplaying Game (Second Edition)
description: Pathfinder Second Edition is a fantasy tabletop RPG that evolved from Dungeons & Dragons 3.5, offering a robust system with tactical depth and extensive character customization. In Pathfinder 2E, players create characters by choosing an ancestry (like Human, Elf, Dwarf, Goblin, etc.), a background (which gives a bit of story and skill boosts, such as “Gladiator” or “Scholar”), and a class (such as Fighter, Wizard, 17 Rogue, Cleric, and many more, including unique ones like Alchemist or Oracle). Characters progress from level 1 to 20, gaining feats and abilities at nearly every level, which allows for fine-tuned builds. The core mechanic uses a twenty-sided die (d20) plus modifiers against a Difficulty Class (DC) to resolve actions, similar to D&D. A highlight of PF2E is its three-action combat economy: each turn, a character has three actions that can be used for anything from swinging a sword, casting a spell (which might take 2 actions, say), moving, raising a shield, etc., plus one free “reaction” per round for things like opportunity attacks or shield blocking. This creates a flexible, fluid combat experience where players have lots of choice in how to spend their turn. The system also introduces the concept of degrees of success: if you beat a DC by 10 or more, it's a critical success; if you fail by 10 or more, it's a critical failure. This means that things like attack rolls, skill checks, and saving throws can have enhanced outcomes (good or bad) beyond simple success/failure. For example, a critical success on a skill check might yield extra information, while a critical failure on a save might have a worse effect. Character building is very modular. Aside from class features, players get Ancestry feats, Class feats, Skill feats, General feats at various levels - each category adding abilities or perks. This feels like plugging pieces into your character as it grows, allowing for, say, two Fighters to diverge significantly if one chooses archery feats and another chooses two-weapon melee feats. Spellcasting in PF2E still uses prepared or spontaneous slots depending on class, but the spells often have scalable effects when cast at higher slot levels. Many spells can be cast with varying action costs for different effects (for instance, the heal spell can be 1, 2, or 3 actions: one action heals touch, two actions heals at range, three actions is a group burst heal). The game places emphasis on balance and clarity; nearly every rule has keyword traits that interact predictably with other rules (e.g., an ability might have the “move” trait, meaning it triggers reactions that look for movement). Outside of combat, PF2E has robust subsystems for exploration (with defined modes like exploration vs downtime) and things like crafting, downtime activities, and even a mode for resolving influence in social situations or hexploration for traveling wilderness. The overall tone and setting of default Pathfinder is high fantasy in the world of Golarion, which has a patchwork of varied regions to accommodate gothic horror, pirate adventures, eastern-inspired fantasy, etc. The game is well-supported with adventure paths (campaigns) that often mix dungeon crawls, wilderness, and intrigue. Playing Pathfinder 2E often appeals to players who enjoy a bit of crunch and tactical combat - it's not as heavy as some systems, but compared to very rules-light games, it has a lot of moving parts. However, these parts interlock to give a great sense of character identity and progression; you really feel your character growing more capable and defined by choices. And GMs get plenty of tools to design encounters, from a rich Bestiary with calibrated monster math to treasure distribution guidelines. In summary, Pathfinder 2E is about heroes facing perilous quests in a mechanically rich playground: you'll slay dragons, navigate treacherous politics, delve into ancient ruins-all supported by a system that makes such exploits both challenging and satisfying through tactical play and character options.

name: Pirate Borg
description: Pirate Borg is a self-contained role-playing game that 18 combines the doom-laden, ultra-simplified rules of Mörk Borg with the swashbuckling, bloodthirsty world of pirates on the high seas. It's essentially “Mörk Borg does Pirates” - meaning characters are scurvy sea dogs and black- hearted buccaneers trying to survive a brutal, cursed Caribbean (or any sea of your choosing) while fending off naval forces, sea monsters, and supernatural curses. The tone, like Mörk Borg, is grimy and darkly humorous; you're not playing noble heroes but rather opportunistic rogues willing to plunder and pillage to prolong their own lives (which may be nasty, brutish, and short). Character creation is quick and random: you roll for stats (usually 4 core ones like Agility, Strength, etc.), choose or roll a class (like the Cutthroat, Buccaneer, Swashbuckler, etc.), which gives you starting abilities and gear. Hit points are minimal and the damage from a flintlock or cutlass can end you fast if you're unlucky. The game uses a d20 roll-under or roll-over system (depending on if it's tackling Mörk Borg's style or an adapted one) - typically, to attack you roll a d20 plus stat trying to beat an opponent's defense, and to avoid attacks you might roll a defense stat. Rolling a 20 is a critical success (usually max damage or some flourish) and a 1 is a fumble (your pistol misfires, you drop your sword, etc.). Being Mörk Borg-derived, it likely encourages creative rulings over strict rules and includes tables for maritime misfortunes, strange island encounters, and loot. Pirate Borg's setting is filled with nods to classic pirate lore but through a grim lens: ghost ships, cursed treasure (à la “dead man's chest”), voodoo magic, sea-beast infested waters, and colonial powers to antagonize or flee from. The game might include a system for naval combat simplified to the basics (ship weapons do big damage, the main goal is usually to cripple the other ship enough to board or escape). But it's not a crunchy simulation; it's more about the chaos and flavor - blasting a broadside and then swinging on ropes to board the enemy deck, cutlass in teeth. Magic, if present, could be in the form of occult rituals or relics (like a compass that points to what you desire most, or a cursed coin that makes you unkillable but decays your flesh). The book likely mirrors Mörk Borg's art-forward zine style, but with pirate maps, skeletal pirates, and rum-splattered pages. In play, a session could see the crew navigating treacherous shoals to find a hidden cove of treasure, only to find the treasure cursed and the dead rising; or being hired by a governor to hunt a notorious undead pirate lord; or simply surviving a sudden hurricane that threatens to dash the ship on rocks (with the crew scrambling to jury-rig repairs and manage flooding). True to its roots, death is a constant threat and mercy is scarce; betrayal can come easy (perhaps one of the PCs even has a secret goal to mutiny and take over). Yet, for all the bleakness, the game revels in the anarchic fun of piracy - players are free to attempt outrageous stunts and acts of cunning. After all, it's better to burn out spectacularly with a cannon fuse in one hand and a bottle of rum in the other than to wither away in some prison cell. In short, Pirate Borg delivers an intense, atmospheric pirate adventure experience where life is cheap, the sea is cruel, and fortune favors the bold (and the lucky). Yarr.

name: RuneQuest: Roleplaying in Glorantha
description: RuneQuest: Roleplaying in Glorantha is a mythic fantasy RPG that immerses players in the richly detailed bronze-age world of Glorantha, where gods and spirits are active forces and humans are often defined by their cults and communities. Players create adventurers who are 19 typically members of a clan or tribe in the region of Dragon Pass or Prax, amid a period of heroic struggle (the epic campaigns often set around the Dragonrise and the wars involving the Lunar Empire). What sets RuneQuest apart is that all player characters have access to magic (either through cults and gods or animist practices) and that personal and cultural identity is deeply ingrained in mechanics (passions like Love (Family) or Hate (Chaos) and Rune affinities like Air, Earth, Fire that influence behavior and magic). The system is a refined version of Basic Role-Playing (percentile-based skills). If you want to swing a sword or cast a spell, you roll under your skill or ability percentage on d100 to succeed. Combat in RuneQuest is gritty and tactical: it features hit locations and devastating criticals. Armor reduces damage (damage is rolled by weapon). A solid blow to the head or a major artery can fell even a powerful warrior. Thus, there is an emphasis on avoiding getting hit (parrying, dodging) and on group tactics. Healing magic exists and is fairly accessible (many cults teach minor healing), but severe wounds or limbs lost to critical hits require powerful intervention or long healing times. One signature element: the use of Runes. Characters have affinity ratings with cosmic Runes (like Air, Beast, Truth, Death) that reflect both their personality and their magical leanings. For example, a high Air rune might mean you're proud, violent, and associated with Orlanth (the storm king god). These runes can augment magic and sometimes be tested to see if a character can align or overcome their nature in certain situations. Cults and gods are central. If you worship, say, Humakt (god of war and death), you'll have access to specific rune spells (like Sever Spirit or Truesword) and a community of worshippers. But you'll also be expected to follow Humakt's strictures (like always keeping oaths and never using healing magic). Magic in RuneQuest comes in three flavors: Spirit Magic (common, personal spells like Bladesharp to enchant a weapon or Heal), Rune Magic (powerful divine miracles granted by the gods, like calling down lightning or resurrecting the dead, which require sacrificing POW (permanent points) to the cult), and Sorcery (less common in Dragon Pass; a more intellectual, manipulation-of-laws-of-nature magic). Adventuring in Glorantha often involves dealing with mythic themes: you might heroquest (enter the realm of the gods to reenact myths to gain boons), broker peace or ignite feuds between clans, fend off Chaos incursions (broo raiders spreading disease, for example), negotiate with ancient spirits or dragonewts, and generally navigate a world where mythology, politics, and daily life are deeply intertwined. The game emphasizes that Glorantha isn't generic fantasy-it's a world with unique creatures (no standard orcs or goblins here, but you have things like troll kin and walktapus), and its societies have realistic concerns (cattle raids, marriages, harvests) alongside the epic (sudden monster attacks, divine interventions). Running or playing RuneQuest rewards immersion in that lore: players who engage with their character's clan, swear by their gods, and use their passions will find it richly rewarding, as the GM is encouraged to weave those elements into scenarios. Overall, RuneQuest offers a grand tapestry of heroic bronze age adventure, where you feel like a tiny mortal amid powerful forces - but with the right magic, allies, and courage, you can carve your saga into the eternal chronicles of the gods. It's lethal, beautiful, and transcendent all at once, as any mythic journey should be." 20

name: Savage Worlds
description: Savage Worlds is a universal tabletop RPG system built for speed, action, and ease of use, encapsulated by its tagline: Fast! Furious! Fun! It's designed to handle any genre-fantasy, pulp, sci-fi, horror, modern thriller -with a consistent set of rules that prioritize quick resolution and cinematic flair. Characters in Savage Worlds are defined by attributes (like Agility, Smarts, Strength, etc.) and skills, both of which are assigned die types (d4, d6, d8, d10, d12; higher is better). If you have a d8 Shooting skill, you roll a d8 when firing a gun. One core twist is that player characters (and key NPCs) are Wild Cards, which means when they roll a trait (skill or attribute), they also roll a Wild Die (d6) and take the higher result. Furthermore, dice “explode” (called acing): if you roll the maximum on a die, you roll it again and add, potentially achieving very high totals. This means even a seemingly weak character can sometimes pull off an amazing feat with a lucky streak. The target for rolls is usually 4 (modified by difficulty). Succeeding by 4 or more (called a “raise”) often gives extra benefits (like more damage or a better outcome). Combat is organized by drawing cards for initiative each round (a fun mechanic that can throw in twists, like Jokers giving bonuses and immediate action). Attacks are opposed by defenses like Parry (for melee) or a static number (for ranged). Damage is compared to a Toughness stat; if damage meets Toughness, the target is Shaken (stunned or rattled), and each raise over Toughness causes a Wound. Average folks have 0 wounds before incapacitation, Wild Cards have 3, so essentially Wild Cards can take a few hits (or one really big hit) before going down, while minor NPCs drop if wounded once (making mooks easy to clear, very pulpy). There's also a Benny system: players get Benny chips which they can spend to re-roll dice, soak damage (attempt to reduce Wounds), or influence narrative (like say they have a useful item or coincidentally know an NPC). This encourages risk-taking and gives players some control when the dice turn ugly. Character advancement is point-based and incremental (called “Advances”), typically allowing either small improvements or new Edges (talents/ feats) every few sessions. The system has many optional subsystems for different situations: quick resolution for chases, mass battles, social conflict, etc., each meant to capture the dramatic high points without bogging down. For example, a “Dramatic Task” might have players trying to defuse a bomb within 3 rounds needing a certain number of successes, with complications on clubs drawn for initiative, etc. Tonally, Savage Worlds leans pulp-action by default: heroes are competent and a bit larger-than-life (Wild Cards and exploding dice make you quite capable), and the mechanics for stun/shaken and Bennies encourage narrative highs and lows that feel like movie beats. It's also miniatures- friendly if one likes (the core rules mention inches for movement and ranges). But it doesn't require a grid - theater of the mind works too. Savage Worlds appeals to groups who like the flexibility to jump genres, or who enjoy a game that can do tactical combat quickly but isn't as heavy as something like D&D 3.5/Pathfinder. It's robust enough to simulate vehicle battles, magic, weird science, superpowers (with expansions), without changing core rules. In a single campaign, your pulp heroes could fight mobsters, pilot a zeppelin, perform an arcane ritual, and chase down a mummy, all with the same fast-playing system. And importantly, the GM can throw lots of fodder enemies at the players (because only Wild Cards roll the extra die and have wounds) which makes the heroes feel 21 like action stars mowing through lesser threats until the real villain shows up. In summary, Savage Worlds is about getting into the action, not sweating small details, and playing out bombastic, cinematic scenes-whether you're cowboys, commandos, or cat-people from Planet X-while still maintaining enough gamey bits to satisfy tactical or character-build cravings in a lighter way.

name: Shadowdark
description: Shadowdark is a fantasy dungeon-crawling RPG designed to blend the old-school feel of early D&D with modern streamlined mechanics. It positions itself as a return to “the dungeon” as a core adventure site, where torches are your lifeline and every shadow could hide danger. Characters in Shadowdark are often created quickly and simply, with classic attributes (likely 3d6 in order or similar for Strength, Dexterity, etc.) and straightforward class choices (Fighter, Thief, Cleric, Wizard reminiscent of B/X era). Hit points are modest, and survivability often comes down to player wit rather than bloated stats. The rules use a d20 for actions: roll high, adding relevant modifiers, aiming to beat a target difficulty or an opponent's armor class for attacks. It's very similar to D&D 5E in base mechanics but stripped down to essentials. However, unlike 5E, Shadowdark has an ethos of resource management and peril. One of its hallmark features is real-time torch tracking: a torch in the game lasts, say, one real-world hour. Players are encouraged to set a timer when they light a torch, upping the tension as you delve deeper and time ticks down. When the timer rings, if you haven't lit a new one, you're in complete darkness (hence the name Shadowdark), which is extremely dangerous. The game also typically forgoes grids and turns outside of combat-exploration is done narratively, with the referee (GM) often asking “What do you do?” in 10-minute intervals and tracking things like wandering monsters. When combat occurs, it's swift and deadly; some iterations use “theater of the mind” range categories (close, near, far) instead of precise grids, and initiative might be group-based or simply alternating, to keep things fluid. Magic in Shadowdark is reminiscent of old- school D&D: wizards can cast a limited number of spells (perhaps prepared or via a spell roll, depending on variant rules), and spells might have dangerous consequences or require casting checks. Clerics channel divine power but might have to beseech their god when out of miracles. Importantly, there's an emphasis on the unknown: players often are not given all details, and must experiment carefully.
