For instance, identifying a potion might require a taste test (and risk), or figuring out a mysterious device might need trial and error. The GM is encouraged to play fairly but let the dice and the players' decisions shape outcomes - if a foolish move is made, deadly results follow. The game also cuts down on “ability bloat.” Instead of long skill lists, it might rely on attribute checks or simply player description to resolve challenges. There might be a Luck stat or luck mechanic to cover miscellaneous fortunes. The tone and artwork of Shadowdark (inspired by classic modules) conjure a sense of stepping into a torchlit corridor where you hear chittering in the dark, your comrades are bleeding and low on spells, and you know you have to find treasure and get out before your light dies or something finds you. It builds tension not through big hero theatrics, but through atmosphere and the ever-present risk of running out of crucial supplies. Yet, it embraces modern convenience by clarifying rules, aiming for cohesive rulings, and allowing things like ascending AC or simple advantage/disadvantage mechanics to speed up play. In essence, Shadowdark is for 22 those who enjoy the suspense, challenge, and simplicity of old-school dungeon adventures, but want a game that's easy to learn and play, with just enough modern polish to remove the clunk. It's about exploring dangerous places with friends, thinking on your feet, and feeling the thrill (and fear) of the dark closing in around you.

name: Shadowrun
description: Shadowrun is a hybrid cyberpunk-fantasy role-playing game set in the dystopian near future (originally 2050s, in later editions 2080s). In this timeline, not only did megacorporations take over and tech advance (cyberware, matrix internet, drones, etc.), but magic also returned to the world in a global event called the Awakening. This caused some humans to goblinize into orks and trolls, babies to be born as dwarfs or elves, and mythological creatures to reappear. The result is a world that's part Gibson-esque cyberpunk and part urban fantasy. Players typically take on the roles of shadowrunners: mercenaries on the fringe of society who take dangerous jobs (legally gray or outright criminal) from corporate fixers, crime bosses, or others who need deniable assets. A team might include street samurai (combat-focused with cybernetic enhancements), deckers (hackers jack into the Matrix via cyberdecks), riggers (remote-control vehicle and drone specialists), magicians (could be hermetic mages or shamanic spellcasters, slinging spells and summoning spirits), adepts (martial artists who use magic internally to enhance their physical abilities), and faces (smooth-talking con artists and negotiators). The game's mechanics (in editions 3–5 for example) use pools of six-sided dice. A character has attributes and skills; for a test, a number of dice equal to attribute + skill are rolled, and each die that meets or exceeds a target number (in earlier editions) or is 5 or 6 (in later editions) counts as a success or “hit.” The number of hits is compared to a threshold or opposed by someone else's hits. Only counting 5s and 6s (target number fixed at 5) with variable thresholds (in 4th/5th edition) streamlined things versus older editions where target numbers could change and dice could “explode.” Combat is detailed and can be very deadly: guns do serious damage, and since you roll a lot of dice, a big pool can overkill someone easily. There are rules for cover, recoil, various ammo types, etc. But also, because of the fantasy element, you could have an ork street samurai with a katana fighting a fireball-flinging mage alongside a drone flying overhead providing cover fire. Shadowrun has multiple “worlds” of action: physical, astral (where mages and spirits interact in a parallel magical plane), and matrix (a virtual reality cyberspace where deckers navigate systems and battle ICE – security programs). In older editions, a big challenge was that deckers would often do their hacking while other players sat idle; newer editions tried to alleviate that by making hacking more Augmented-Reality and able to be done alongside the team or by giving others something to do. Still, a good Shadowrun team synchronizes these aspects: maybe the decker loops cameras and opens doors while the rigger overrides the security drone and the mage banishes an interfering spirit, all as the street sam and adept handle the goons on the ground. Magic in Shadowrun follows specific traditions; spells are learned and have drain (the more powerful the spell, the more it can hurt or fatigue the caster). Summoning spirits is a big part (shamans summon nature spirits, hermetics summon elementals, etc.) and those spirits can be very powerful allies. There's also the risk of cyberware: while cyber implants give 23 big advantages (boosted reflexes, implanted guns, datajacks in your head to interface with machines), they cost Essence, which represents life energy; if you lose too much Essence to cyberware, your ability to do magic (if you had any) is basically gone and even your humanity is dulled (not mechanically like Humanity in Cyberpunk 2020, but narratively). The setting is a huge draw: mega- sprawls like Seattle (the default city) are filled with neon lights, holographic ads, biker gangs, Yakuza, and elves in trench coats; Native American nations reclaimed large parts of North America; dragons run corporations (literally a great dragon is a CEO); the world is a mess of high-tech and awakened forests and folklore. Shadowruns themselves are missions often starting with a fixer hiring the team, doing legwork (gathering intel on the target), planning, then executing usually with a mix of stealth, hacking, maybe a fast-talking con, and inevitably some combat when things go sideways. The tone can range from dark and deadly serious (corporations committing atrocities and you trying to survive in the cracks) to campy and wild (troll rock stars and orc street gangs with magic graffiti). Underlying it is usually an anti-authoritarian, anti-establishment vibe: you live in the shadows because you reject or can't be part of the hyper- controlled system the corps built. You run to gain freedom, creds, or just because you're a misfit with unique talents. In summary, Shadowrun is both a mash-up and a unique genre of its own: imagine The Matrix meets Lord of the Rings meets Blade Runner meets a crime heist movie.

name: Star Trek Adventures
description: Star Trek Adventures is a science fiction role- playing game that allows players to assume the roles of Starfleet officers (or possibly allies) exploring the galaxy and upholding the ideals of the Federation as seen in the Star Trek universe. The game focuses on teamwork, problem- solving, and moral dilemmas rather than combat for combat's sake (though space battles and phaser fights can certainly occur). It uses Modiphius's 2d20 system: for any task, a character rolls 2 (or more) d20s and tries to get as many successes as possible by rolling under their Attribute + Discipline combination (attributes are things like Control, Daring, etc., and Disciplines are the Starfleet branches like Security, Science, Engineering, etc.). Difficulty ranges from 0 (very easy) up to 5 (incredibly hard), indicating how many successes are needed. If you roll more successes than needed, you generate Momentum, a group resource that can be spent to obtain extra benefits, like more information from a scan or an extra action in combat. The GM likewise has Threat, a pool they can use to make challenges tougher or introduce complications. The rules encourage a flow where players might bank Momentum from an easy encounter to spend in a tougher situation later, mimicking the building drama of a Star Trek episode. Characters are typically on a Federation starship. They might be the bridge crew - a Captain, a Chief Engineer, a Science Officer, Doctor, etc. - and adventures (structured in “episodes”) can range from diplomatic negotiations and scientific investigations to responding to distress signals and confronting hostile forces like Klingons or Romulans (depending on era; the core game leans Next Gen era but supports all). The system handles personal combat (phasers set to stun, 24 cover and minor actions, etc.) but firefights are usually quick and decisive as in the shows. There's also a system for starship combat, where each player often takes on a ship role (one might man sensors, another the helm, another tactical, etc.) and the ship's capabilities are statted out, with decisions about power allocation, shield modulation, and maneuvers. Star Trek Adventures really emphasizes the “story” and “values” of characters. Each character has Values - short phrases that describe their principles (like “Never leave a crew member behind” or “There's a technical solution to every problem”). These can be invoked to get bonuses or re-rolls when relevant, but can also be challenged for rewards when the story pushes the character to act against a Value or re- evaluate it (character growth). This ties into the common Star Trek theme of personal beliefs tested by extraordinary circumstances. The game also encourages a format of play that mirrors the TV shows: an introduction (maybe mysterious or tense), rising challenges, maybe an A and B plot for the session, and a climax that often involves a creative or diplomatic solution as much as, if not more than, a combat one. The Prime Directive and Federation ideals are often at play in adventures: scenarios might involve choosing between saving a pre-warp civilization or obeying orders, negotiating peace between feuding planets, or grappling with the moral implications of new technology. The system's Momentum/ Threat and Values help play out these dramatic moments by giving mechanical weight to bold actions and ethical stands. Overall, Star Trek Adventures strives to capture that optimistic, inquiry-driven spirit of Star Trek. It's about cooperation (players really benefit from helping each other succeed with assists), both among the crew and with those they meet; it's about using science, compassion, and ingenuity to solve problems; and it's about boldly going where no one has gone before, experiencing the wonders of a vast galaxy. With this game, you can reenact the feel of an episode or movie: one session might be tense ship combat against Romulans in a nebula, the next a courtroom drama defending a crewmate accused of a crime on an alien world, and another a puzzling scientific anomaly that threatens a colony. All in a day's work for Starfleet's finest.

name: Star Wars Roleplaying Game
description: Star Wars Roleplaying Game (by Fantasy Flight Games) is an RPG that captures the cinematic adventure of the Star Wars universe, allowing players to take on roles such as smugglers, rebels, Jedi-in- training, bounty hunters, or other iconic archetypes. It uses a narrative dice system with custom polyhedral dice that have symbols instead of numbers. When you attempt an action, you assemble a dice pool of positive dice (based on your character's skill and situational advantages) and negative dice (based on difficulty and situational drawbacks) and roll them all together. The symbols are then tallied: Successes vs. Failures and Advantage vs. Threat (and occasionally Triumph vs. Despair, which are special symbols). If successes outnumber failures, the action succeeds; if not, it fails. But the Advantage/ Threat and Triumph/Despair can introduce side effects regardless of success. For example, you might fail to shoot the stormtrooper (failure) but generate Advantage that allows your next ally a clear shot, or you succeed at fixing the hyperdrive (success) but with Threat that means it took longer than expected and TIE Fighters are closing in. This system allows for results that drive story twists and turns, much like scenes in the films. The game is split into three 25 core sub-lines (all fully compatible): Edge of the Empire (scoundrels and fringe life), Age of Rebellion (military and Rebels vs Empire), and Force and Destiny (Jedi and Force users in the dark times of the Empire). But characters from any can mix; it's common to have a group with, say, a brash pilot (Edge), a Bothan spy (Age), a fallen apprentice with a lightsaber (Force and Destiny), and maybe a droid mechanic. Character creation uses broad careers and specializations (e.g., Bounty Hunter - Gadgeteer, or Soldier - Pilot, or Consular - Healer) that give access to talent trees (abilities to buy) and set initial skills. The feeling is very “Star Wars”: attributes and skills are straightforward (pilot, blaster, lore, persuasion, etc.), and characters are competent but not invincible. A starting character might be able to take down a few minions or talk past a guard, but still has to be careful; by the time they progress, they can pull off more outrageous stunts, survive bigger hits, and so on. Combat is fluid: no grid by default, using range bands abstractly (Engaged, Short, Medium, etc.). A hit with a blaster can incapacitate a typical mook in one shot (very cinematic). PCs and important NPCs have a Wound threshold and Strain threshold (a bit like hit points and stamina/mental stress). Lightsabers are deadly; they roll a lot of damage and pierce armor, so a lightsaber-wielding character is scary (but attracting Imperial attention, which is intentional balance). Force powers are available mostly to Force and Destiny characters and work via a system of generating Force points (rolling special Force dice to see how much power you can channel, possibly having to flirt with the dark side to get enough oomph). The narrative dice truly shine in things like starship chases or complex actions: you might roll to navigate an asteroid field and succeed with a Triumph (meaning not only do you evade the TIEs, but maybe you discover a shortcut to your destination). Or in social encounters, a failure with Advantage might mean the diplomat NPC rejects your argument but lets slip crucial info in the process. The GM is encouraged to use these cues to keep the story dynamic, much like a director cutting between action, comedy, and drama beats. Another neat mechanic is Destiny Points: a pool of light side and dark side points represented by tokens. Players can flip a light side point to dark to upgrade one of their dice or declare a setting detail (“Conveniently, there's a hovercart here we can use to escape!”). The GM can flip dark to light to upgrade difficulty or introduce complications. It's a tug-of-war that ensures everyone has some narrative influence and that the Force (or fate) is always in motion. Ultimately, Star Wars RPG by FFG is about collaborative storytelling in a galaxy far, far away, where rules facilitate the feel of the movies - daring escapades, desperate gunfights, high-speed chases, tense negotiations, and the ever-present battle between hope and despair (light and dark). It's cinematic, forgiving of crazy ideas, and actively pushes for descriptions and creativity, making each session feel like you're playing through a new Star Wars adventure on par with the films or series.

name: Starfinder
description: Starfinder is a science-fantasy role-playing game that takes the concepts of Pathfinder (classic fantasy RPG evolved from D&D 3.5) and propels them into a far-future space opera setting. It mixes high-tech gadgetry and starship combat with elements of magic and weird planar mysteries. The core setting is the Pact Worlds, a solar system with a coalition of diverse planets (including futuristic city-world Absalom Station, the harsh desert of Akiton, 26 the undead-ruled Eox, etc.) bound by treaties. In Starfinder, players can be humans or a variety of alien species (many brand-new, like the ratlike Ysoki, insectoid Shirrens, reptilian Vesk, etc., along with fantasy staples that have evolved in space, like elves and dwarves). Classes are a blend of sci-fi and magic: you have Soldiers (straight-up fighters, mercenaries), Technomancers (techno-wizards who cast magic through understanding of science), Mechanics (gearheads who often have a robotic drone or an AI “exocortex”), Envoys (charismatic leaders and medics), Operatives (spies and stealth specialists), Solarians (mystic warriors who harness stars' energy, kind of space paladins/ monks), and more via expansions. The mechanics are derived from D20/Pathfinder: d20 roll high for attacks and skill checks, classes with levels and Stamina/Hit Points, Feats, etc., but streamlined in some parts (for example, Starfinder condensed Pathfinder's skill list and uses a unified experience table for leveling). Combat can be on grid or theater of mind, but it involves ranged weapons (guns have different ranges, some do energy damage vs. kinetic, etc.) and melee (yes, you can have laser swords or analog melee weapons like tactical swords). Armor in Starfinder gives two types of AC: Energy (EAC) and Kinetic (KAC) to defend against different attack types. PCs have Resolve Points which fuel certain abilities and allow them to stabilize or get back up from near death quickly (to keep action moving). Perhaps the most distinctive subsystem is starship combat: the party typically has a starship and during starship encounters each player can take a role (Captain, Pilot, Engineer, Gunner, Science Officer, etc.) and on each round, after a piloting initiative, they perform actions in a sequence (engineers boost shields, science officers scan or target lock, pilot maneuvers, gunners fire, etc.). It's like a separate tactical minigame using a hex map where facing and weapon arcs matter. It plays a bit like a cooperative board game where the ship's performance is tied to their combined efforts and skill checks. Magic exists, but in a science-fantasy twist, it's treated almost like another branch of physics that's been incorporated into society: there are still spellcasters (Technomancers and Solarians and some Mystics from expansions), and magic items (called “fusions” to augment weapons, spell gems to cast spells, etc.), but you'll also see androids with mystical programming or hackers who use scrolls that are actually code. The game strongly supports ranged combat and mobility (jetpacks! zero-g!) as well as star travel, exploration of planets, and interacting with alien cultures. The tone of Starfinder ranges from pulpy adventure (treasure-hunting derelict space hulks, smuggling runs) to military (fighting the insectile Swarm invasion or skirmishes with the Veskarium empire before they allied) to noir (corporate espionage in Absalom Station's shadows) to straight bizarre (visiting the Drift, a hyperspace plane where pieces of other planes show up when using faster-than-light travel). The lore introduced concepts like “The Gap,” a mysterious temporal blackout where history before a certain point is lost (including what happened to Golarion, the Pathfinder fantasy world - its planet is missing from the Pact Worlds, replaced by Absalom Station). This gives a sense of mystery and openness to the setting for GMs. With high-tech gear, you'll have things like personal shield devices, cybernetics, and computers to hack, alongside encountering space-dragons or plasma elementals. A crew could consist of a Vesk soldier with a machine gun, a Lashunta technomancer wielding spells and a laser pistol, a 27 Ysoki mechanic with a robot drone, and a Human envoy talking their way past security - all aboard their trusty starship with a Drift engine to jump between stars. In summary, Starfinder is all about merging the crunch and character depth of a Pathfinder-style system with the expansive, colorful world of sci-fi: players get to level up, optimize and loot gear, but also fly starships, negotiate with aliens, solve mysteries of ancient tech, and blast foes with magic and lasers in equal measure.

name: Symbaroum
description: Symbaroum is a dark fantasy role-playing game with a strong focus on atmosphere, exploration of an ancient world, and the corrupting nature of power (especially magic). The setting is the kingdom of Ambria and the vast, mysterious forest of Davokar to its north. Ambria is a fledgling kingdom established by humans fleeing a devastated land after a great war. To survive and prosper, many Ambrians venture into Davokar - a forest that was once home to the long-fallen empire of Symbaroum - to find treasure, artifacts, and resources. But Davokar is filled with dangerous creatures and vengeful spirits, and it's the sacred domain of the indigenous barbarian clans and ancient elves who guard its depths. In Symbaroum, players often take the roles of treasure- hunters, explorers, or agents of factions (like the Queen's Rangers, Ambrian nobles, or witches of the barbarian clans) heading into the forest or dealing with its threats. The system is relatively simple: it's d20 roll-under for actions. Each character has attributes (Accurate, Cunning, Discreet, Persuasive, Quick, Resolute, Strong, Vigilant) typically ranging up to 15 or so. To succeed on an action, you want to roll a d20 and get equal to or lower than your relevant attribute (modified by difficulty or enemy stat). One neat twist: often the player rolls everything. If a character attacks an enemy, they'd roll against their Accurate modified by the enemy's Defense; if an enemy attacks the player, the player rolls against their own Defense (Quick or Vigilant attribute, depending on situation) modified by the enemy's Accurate. So if the roll succeeds, it means the defender (player) avoided harm; if it fails, the defender gets hit. Damage is dealt and reduced by armor (which can also have special properties). Characters are defined by their abilities and powers rather than a strict class system. They might have Martial abilities (like Quick Draw or Massive Damage), Mystical powers (if they're a theurg or sorcerer or witch, like spells and rituals), or Social abilities (like Iron Fist for intimidation or Captivating Song). These abilities have tiers (Novice, Adept, Master) granting bigger effects. Combat can be deadly; HP (actually “Toughness”) is often not high, so a couple of sword blows or one nasty monster strike can take a player down. One of the core thematic mechanics is corruption. When characters use magic or certain mystical artifacts, or sometimes just by being in blighted areas of Davokar, they accrue corruption (temporary and possibly permanent). If their corruption ever equals or exceeds their Resolute, they risk horrible effects - basically their bodies or minds start being warped by dark energy. This is to reflect how Symbaroum's magic is not free: it has a cost, and delving too deep (or getting too greedy in the forest) literally taints you. The setting's tension lies between Ambrians pushing into Davokar for treasure and territory, and the natives (barbarians and their witch mystics, and ancient beings like the elves) trying to prevent another dark empire like old Symbaroum from arising and awaking the slumbering evils in the forest. So, campaigns often 28 involve exploring ruins (dungeon crawl style) and dealing with factions: maybe you work for the Queen to map an area, but you also have to negotiate or fight a barbarian clan that sees you as violators. Or perhaps the party themselves are outlaws or explorers just looking to get rich off forgotten artifacts, while trying not to get corrupted by the magic within them. The tone is melancholic, eerie, and tense. The forest Davokar is almost a character itself - an ever- present looming threat and temptation, full of riches and horrors. The art of the game is gorgeous and reinforces this with dark, moody depictions of moss- covered statues, fang-filled shadows, and weary adventurers. In summary, Symbaroum offers a fairly straightforward rules system with some unique twists, embedded in a rich, original setting where every venture into the unknown has the potential to reward you with golden treasure or curse you forever (or both). It's about the clash of civilizations, the seduction of power, and the struggle to maintain your humanity (or Ambrianity) in a world that has seen countless tragedies unfold under the canopies of the ancient woods.

name: Tales from the Loop
description: Tales from the Loop is a nostalgic sci-fi role- playing game that lets players experience adventures as kids in the 1980s (or 90s) that never were. It's inspired by the artwork of Simon Stålenhag: an alternate history where massive particle accelerators (“Loops”) have been built (in Sweden and in the US) which have led to weird phenomena and technological wonders like robots and floating magnets, all against the backdrop of everyday life. Think of movies and shows like E.T., Stranger Things, Stand By Me, or The Goonies: it's about young friends investigating strange mysteries adults either ignore or dismiss. Players create kids aged 10-15, choosing an archetype like Bookworm, Jock, Popular Kid, Weirdo, etc. Characters have key stats (like Body, Tech, Heart, Mind) and a set of skills under them. The system uses six-sided dice pools (Year Zero Engine): you roll a number of d6 equal to stat+skill, and any 6 rolled is a success. Most tasks only need 1 success; harder ones might need 2 or more. Typically you either succeed or you can fail forward (maybe succeed at a cost or with a condition). If you fail, you can choose to “push” the roll (re-roll failures) at the risk of taking a condition. Conditions like Scared, Exhausted, Injured etc. give a -1 to future rolls and if you have too many, your kid is “Broken” (they collapse or otherwise can't continue until they get help). One big feature: kids in Tales from the Loop cannot die. The stakes can be emotional or about solving the mystery or saving others, but the game assumes a kind of safety net for the kids themselves (this encourages players to take risks they might not if death were on the table, fitting the genre). To balance that, conditions and failures tend to create complications for the story or might temporarily remove a kid from action. The game emphasizes that the kids have everyday lives: you have a home life with one or more NPC parents (who have their own issues), maybe siblings, homework, chores, etc. So often a session might start after school, investigating a weird incident in the woods, but then you have to be home by dinner or you'll get grounded. The tension between mundane life and the extraordinary Loop mysteries is a core theme. To support character depth, each kid has things like a Problem (e.g. “Dad's an alcoholic”), a Pride (some trait they're proud of, like “I'm the smartest in my class” which they can invoke to get an automatic success once per session), and a favorite song (the game encourages making a mixtape of 80s music!). They also have a 29 Hideout-collectively, the kids have a secret place they hang out (like a treehouse or an abandoned car in the junkyard) which is safe from adults and can be used to rest and heal conditions by roleplaying scenes of camaraderie (like commiserating about troubles or helping each other out). Adventures (called Mysteries) follow a formula akin to an episode of a show: there's a mystery that starts small (strange lights, a lost robot, a weird science teacher acting odd) and escalates. The kids investigate different locations (using both roleplay and skill checks), meet NPCs who might be friendly, weird, or secretive, and eventually piece together what's happening (perhaps a malfunction at the Loop has caused time anomalies, or a rogue AI is controlling farm equipment, etc.). Finally there's a showdown or climax where the kids likely solve the big problem. Then life goes somewhat back to normal, with maybe a touching or reflective scene at the end. There is also a mechanic for “extended trouble” which is like a group challenge where everyone contributes successes to overcome a larger obstacle, which is often used for the climax (like escaping a flooding facility-everyone must help). The tone is really about wonder and adolescent resilience. Adults rarely believe the kids, or they're too busy with their own dramas (in the 80s, every parent is either at work or struggling with something), so the kids are largely on their own, relying on friendship. In game, that translates to kids can help each other with rolls, and there's no PvP conflict-it's assumed the party works together. Tales from the Loop sessions weave between scenes of kids biking around the lake or sharing candy at their hideout, and scenes of tracking a strange creature or hacking a futuristic computer, then maybe back to arguing with your sibling at home or trying to avoid getting grounded after sneaking out. It's charming, a bit spooky but not outright horror (more “mysteries with a sense of wonder”), and heavily leans on 80s nostalgia and the idea that the world is full of strange, sometimes beautiful, sometimes dangerous things that children, with their open minds, are best suited to discover.

name: Tales of the Valiant
description: Tales of the Valiant is a fantasy role-playing game developed by Kobold Press, built on the core rules of 5th Edition D&D under the codename Project Black Flag. It aims to provide a familiar 5E experience with some fresh twists and Kobold Press's own flavorful design. In Tales of the Valiant, players create heroic characters from classic fantasy lineages (races) and choose classes very akin to the D&D archetypes (fighter, wizard, rogue, cleric, etc., though often renamed or slightly reimagined to avoid WotC's proprietary terms). For example, a fighter might be called a Warrior, a wizard a Mage. The game keeps the beloved 5E core: the six ability scores (Strength, Dexterity, etc.), a d20-based resolution (roll a d20, add modifiers, try to meet or beat a Difficulty Class), and hit points, levels, armor class, etc. However, one of the big goals of Tales of the Valiant is to offer more flexibility and modular options in character creation and progression. Kobold Press has introduced the concept of “Talent Trees” which break down class features and feats into thematic groups that players can choose from as they level, allowing for more customized builds without overwhelming choice paralysis. Essentially, 30 instead of every character of a class getting the exact same feature at a given level, they might have a tree with branches and can decide which branch to follow (e.g., a Rogue might choose between more stealth talents vs. swashbuckler combat talents vs. burglary talents). The game also revamps some core mechanics like spells and magic to incorporate Kobold Press's own spells and possibly tweak things that fans found problematic in 5E (like maybe addressing balance issues or giving martial classes more interesting options). Because it's born from the Open 5E SRD, Tales of the Valiant is fully compatible with existing 5E adventures and monsters, which means you can pick up any Kobold Press adventure or even a Wizards' adventure and run it with minimal conversion. However, it also introduces new content: Kobold Press has a reputation for their creature design and Midgard setting, so expect rich new monsters, some new magic subsystem perhaps (like their approach to magic might include minor rituals or a different take on spellcasting cooldowns), and possibly tweaks to rest and resources to make pacing different. The tone of Tales of the Valiant is high fantasy and heroic. The name implies that it's about courageous adventurers doing valiant deeds, likely with an emphasis on storytelling and narrative- driven play (Kobold Press adventures usually encourage clever play and have strong story elements). It's not trying to be an OSR gritty reboot; it's more a continuation of the fun, cinematic style of 5E but maybe with crunchier character options (Kobold Press knows their audience often likes a bit of complexity and depth). For example, rather than simplifying, they might add subsystems like more interesting exploration rules or variant encounter rules to address things folks wanted more of in 5E. Also, expect inclusive design and modern sensibilities in terms of lore-Kobold Press has a diverse creative team and likely is building a game that appeals to the broad 5E fanbase. In play, Tales of the Valiant should feel much like D&D 5E: you roll initiative, fight monsters, cast spells like Fireball (perhaps slightly rebalanced or with an alternate upgrade), and solve problems in character. But players might remark, “Oh cool, at level 3 I get to choose from these three different talent trees for my Ranger-do I focus on Beast Mastery, Spellcasting, or Hunting talents?” Or, “Instead of the generic Advantage on this trait, Kobold Press gave my lineage a unique once-per-rest ability that ties into lore.” Essentially, it's aiming to be the evolution of 5E outside of WotC's hands, keeping what worked, adjusting what didn't, and adding original polish. Many might use it as their core going forward for 5E-style gaming since it will be open and community-supported. In summary, Tales of the Valiant is a fresh-yet-familiar fantasy RPG that carries forward the legacy of 5E D&D, packed with new options and refinements to empower players and GMs in telling heroic tales, all under the banner of Kobold Press's high-quality design and art.

name: The Dark Eye
description: The Dark Eye (originally \"Das Schwarze Auge\" in German) is a long-running fantasy role-playing game with a highly detailed setting and robust, simulationist mechanics. It takes place in the richly-developed world of Aventuria, which features diverse regions akin to medieval and Renaissance Europe and beyond. Players create heroes of various backgrounds and professions- knightly warriors, stealthy rogues, learned mages, devout clerics, or even common folk-each defined by a range of attributes, skills, advantages, and disadvantages that allow for deep customization. The game uses a percentile 31 (d100) system but with a unique twist: when attempting a skill, a player rolls three d20s, each corresponding to one of three attributes tied to that skill (for example, a crafting test might check Intelligence, Dexterity, and Strength). The player can then allocate points from their skill rating to offset any dice that rolled above their attribute values. If all three checks succeed after using available skill points, the action succeeds (with remaining skill points indicating quality of success). This mechanic rewards well-rounded characters and adds a strategic layer to skill use. Combat in The Dark Eye is tactical and can be deadly: characters parry and dodge incoming attacks with their own rolls, and damage is mitigated by armor but can still quickly incapacitate an unarmored or outmatched foe. Critical hits and wounds can lead to lasting injuries, reinforcing a sense of realism. Magic and divine miracles exist but are governed by numerous rules to maintain balance and believability- spellcasters have to carefully manage their arcane energy, and invoking the gods can come with strictures. The game's extensive lore and breadth of source material mean that adventures can range from dungeon crawls and monster hunts to courtly intrigue or exploration of unknown lands. Role-playing and character development are strongly emphasized: characters grow not by levels but by spending experience points to improve skills or learn new abilities over time. All these elements combine to create an immersive experience where thoughtful play is rewarded and the fantasy world feels alive and responsive to the characters' actions.

name: The One Ring Roleplaying Game
description: The One Ring Roleplaying Game (2nd Edition by Free League) is an officially licensed RPG set in J.R.R. Tolkien's Middle- earth, focusing on the years between The Hobbit and The Lord of the Rings (around 20th century of the Third Age). It aims to capture the atmosphere of the books: the heroism of humble individuals, the ever-present shadow of evil rising, and the importance of hope, fellowship, and courage. Players form a Company of adventurers coming from cultures of the Wild (like Hobbits of the Shire, Men of Bree or Rohan or Gondor, Dwarves of the Lonely Mountain, Elves of Lindon or Mirkwood, etc.). Each culture has its distinctive traits and starting package (e.g., Hobbits are sneaky and resilient to corruption). Instead of classes, characters have callings (like Scholar, Treasure Hunter, Slayer, Warden, etc.) which guide their motivations and some abilities. The system uses special dice: a 12-sided Feat die and 6-sided Success dice. On the Feat die, one side has the Gandalf rune (automatically succeeds) and one side has the Eye of Sauron (counts as zero and often triggers bad effects). Success dice added are equal to your skill rating; any rolled 6s on these indicate great or extraordinary success if you succeed overall. The target number for a roll is often based on your own attributes (to reflect task difficulty relative to your capability) or a set TN for combat. Characters can spend Hope points to add their Attribute to a roll, a precious resource reflecting their resolve and inner strength. Combat is abstract but tactical: players choose stances (forward, open, defensive, rearward) which affect how often you act and how easy it is to hit or be hit. Damage reduces Endurance, and taking a hit above your tolerance can cause wounds. It's deadly to go toe-to-toe without thought; often, you might parley or escape if outmatched. A major theme is traveling: the game has a Journey system where traveling across the map is an integral part of the 32 story, with players making roles (Guide, Scout, Hunter, Look-out) and facing potential hazards or advantages en route (like terrible weather, friendly encounters, or exhaustion). This system makes the landscape feel present – the world of Middle-earth itself is a character. Another crucial aspect is Corruption: encountering the Shadow (through dreadful places, acts of vice like greed, dealing with dark artifacts or the enemy) can burden characters with Shadow points. If their Shadow points exceed their Hope (or a threshold), they have a Bout of Madness (temporary misbehavior or despair) and potentially gain a permanent Shadow-scar (a negative trait like dragon-sickness greed or grumbling cynicism). Long term, it's possible to fall to the Shadow and retire a character if they accumulate too much corruption. This mechanic reinforces the moral theme of Tolkien's work: staying true to virtues and resisting temptation. Structure- wise, gameplay alternates between Adventuring phases (going on quests, dealing with threats) and Fellowship phases (downtime at a safe haven like Rivendell or the Shire where characters can heal, train, consult patrons like Gandalf, strengthen fellowship, or pursue personal goals). This is where they also reduce Shadow, reflect, and get the feel of time passing (often each fellowship phase is the winter between adventuring seasons). The game emphasizes that you're not supermen; you're relatively ordinary (especially if playing Hobbits or Men) and the great powers of the world might occasionally help you, but often you do what little you can in your corner. Every adventurer has a sense of belonging (to home or people) that grounds them and a destiny or drive that spurs them. The tone is poignant and brave: expect moments of wonder (an Elf city, meeting the Dunedain), fear (the creeping dread of a barrow or an agents of the Enemy), and heartfelt camaraderie (sharing stories by the fire, the joy of returning home with tales to tell). Free League's edition specifically has streamlined some rules from the first edition to make it more accessible, but it keeps the unique dice and flavor. The art and writing drip with respect for Tolkien's world. In play, you might guard the Old Forest Road, negotiate with Beornings and Dwarves to reopen trade, discover a foul plot of Orcs in the Misty Mountains and halt it, all while seeing how these small deeds tie into the larger tapestry of Middle-earth's history. It truly tries to give you the experience of \"stepping into the books\" with your own characters. It's not about accumulating loot or power for power's sake; it's about safeguarding what you love from encroaching darkness, if only for a little while, and earning a song or two about your bravery.

name: Vampire: The Masquerade
description: Vampire: The Masquerade is a modern gothic-punk horror role-playing game about personal horror and political intrigue among vampires. Players take on the roles of vampires (called Kindred) who struggle to maintain their humanity while navigating the complex and dangerous society of the undead. Set in a world much like our own (the World of Darkness), it's a place of corruption, darkness, and hidden supernatural threats. The core themes revolve around the beast within (the feral instincts and hunger for blood all vampires harbor), the so-called “Masquerade” (a global effort by vampires to hide their existence from humans), and the complex social hierarchies (sects like the Camarilla and Anarchs, clans with unique powers and curses, etc.). Mechanically, it uses the Storyteller/Storytelling system: characters have Attributes and Skills rated from 1-5, and form dice pools of d10s. In older 33 editions, you aimed to roll under a Difficulty on each die; in the latest 5th edition, you look for successes (dice showing 6 or higher) and count them, needing more successes for harder tasks. If you get no successes and a die shows a 1 (in older editions) or if you roll more 1s than successes (in some versions), you could botch (critical failure). In 5th edition, hunger is a central mechanic: instead of blood points, hunger dice replace some regular dice in your pool; if they come up successes or failures in certain ways, they can cause you to lose control or display vampiric behavior even if you succeed. Character creation involves choosing a Clan, which gives inherent Disciplines (powers) and weaknesses. For instance, Brujah are passionate and quick to anger (often getting bonuses to physical prowess but trouble resisting frenzy), Tremere are warlocks (blood sorcery but cursed by a blood bond hierarchy), Nosferatu are hideous but masters of stealth, etc. There are 13 major clans, each with unique flavor. Characters also have things like Generation (how far removed from the first vampire, which affects power), but in 5th ed, generation is de-emphasized in favor of Blood Potency and Hunger mechanics. A big part of gameplay is balancing your Hunger (you need to feed on blood; if you don't, hunger grows and you risk frenzy) versus maintaining the Masquerade and your human relationships. You also have a Humanity rating which measures how much empathy and moral sense you have left. Committing evil acts (like murdering for food) can reduce Humanity, making it harder to relate to humans and easier to fall to the Beast (frenzy, degeneration). Socially, vampires are usually part of a sect: the Camarilla (traditionalists who enforce the Masquerade and have princes ruling cities), the Anarchs (rebellious younger Kindred rejecting elder tyranny), or others like the Sabbat (in older editions, a monstrous sect that revels in being vampires and fights Gehenna, the end of days). Much of the intrigue in a chronicle (campaign) stems from interactions with these factions and navigating the plans of elder vampires who use younger ones as pawns. Storylines often involve solving problems for or fighting against these figures: maybe investigating who's been breaching the Masquerade in your city, dealing with a rogue hunter, stopping a Sabbat pack, or negotiating between warring factions. The mood is typically dark and mature: personal tragedies, ethical dilemmas (do you risk your soul to protect your unlife? Is it okay to kill an innocent to ensure your city's safety?), and the seductive nature of power. Combat with Disciplines can be intense (supernatural speed, strength, mind control, etc., make fights very dangerous), but combat is usually a choice to be weighed, not jumped into lightly, as open violence can attract human attention or ruin carefully laid plans. Vampire encourages a lot of player agency in shaping goals - some may crave to hold territory or influence in mortal society, others to uncover secrets of their vampiric curse, others to exact revenge on an elder who wronged them. The GM (Storyteller) weaves a narrative that plays off these ambitions and the setting's threats. It's not a game to “win” so much as to explore a personal story of monstrous transformation (or resistance to it). Sessions might include negotiation scenes, investigations, the occasional desperate scuffle, feeding scenes that reveal something about the character's humanity, and frequent impromptu meetings in Elysium (neutral ground) where social sparring between rivals occurs via clever barbs and Status maneuvering. Overall, Vampire: The Masquerade is about tragedy and horror on an intimate 34 scale - you are a predator that looks like a person, in a society of predators wearing civilized masks, and you must find your way and cling to (or abandon) your remaining scruples as the nights of unlife go on.

name: Vaesen
description: Vaesen is a Nordic horror and mystery RPG set in an alternate 19th-century Scandinavia (primarily Sweden) where the folklore creatures of myth (the “vaesen”) are real, though invisible to most humans. Players are people who possess “The Sight,” an ability to perceive vaesen, often gained after a traumatic or supernatural event. Having the Sight inevitably draws the characters into conflicts involving these creatures. The tone is dark, atmospheric, and investigative, much like a fairy tale by way of gothic horror. Characters in Vaesen are typically members of or associates of a “Society” based out of a haunted mansion (which they gradually restore and improve). The Society's aim is to research and deal with vaesen sightings and incidents, perhaps to protect humanity, or to resolve misunderstandings between humans and vaesen, or to stop malicious creatures. Characters have archetypes like “Doctor,” “Hunter,” “Officer,” “Servant,” etc., each providing a set of skills and a special talent. The Year Zero Engine underpins Vaesen: players roll a number of d6 equal to their relevant Attribute + Skill; 6s are successes, and typically one success is enough, more can improve outcome. If none show 6, it's a failure, and players can choose to “push” the roll by re-rolling failures at the cost of taking a condition (physical or mental like Exhausted, Angry, etc.). Conditions give -1 per condition on future rolls, and if you have too many (4+) you become “Broken,” basically out of action or vulnerable until you recover. It's deadly to face violence unprepared: combat uses the same dice system; weapons and vaesen attacks can deal conditions or worse. Gunshots, claws, etc., can incapacitate quickly. Thus, directly fighting a troll or a giant or even a vengeful ghost without preparation is dangerous. The design encourages investigation and problem-solving: typically each case (scenario) involves a mystery around a vaesen causing some disruption or tragedy. The players travel to a remote village or estate, talk to locals (who might be tight-lipped or superstitious), gather clues (footprints, old legends, someone afflicted by a curse), maybe witness the vaesen's effects (cows dying, child missing, weird song in the woods), then piece together what type of creature it is (each has unique weaknesses or requirements to put to rest). They might need to perform a ritual, obtain a special item (like a grindstone that can sharpen a weapon to harm a troll, or find the bones of a murdered woman to appease a haunt), or negotiate with the creature (some vaesen are intelligent and can be reasoned or bargained with if approached properly). Combat, if it happens, is often more about fending off or surviving long enough to complete some task (like closing a gateway or burning the binding object of a spirit) than just whittling down hit points. The types of vaesen come from Scandinavian folklore: trolls, nixies (water spirits), tomtes (house gnomes), näcken (brook horse), ghosts, lindworms, etc., each with their lore and typical behavior. They aren't all evil; many are simply following their nature or responding to encroachment or wrongs done by humans (cutting down a sacred grove, or breaking a promise). So the game often has a bit of moral complexity: Do you slay the creature? Or try to satisfy it by fixing what humans did wrong? The campaign structure (if using the mansion) also has a bit of group resource management: the Society's headquarters can be 35 upgraded in the downtime between mysteries, adding things like a library (to get research bonuses), a stable (for travel ease), an infirmary (heal faster), etc. This gives a sense of progression and a hub for the characters. Themes of Vaesen include the transition from old rural ways to modern industrial society (the 19th century setting has railroads, factories, social change looming) and how that clash impacts the vaesen who belonged to the old world. There's a melancholic undertone; many vaesen are fading or angry because their place in the world is threatened. The player characters stand somewhat in between: gifted (or cursed) with Sight, they recognize both the human and spirit world sides. This can put them at odds with human authority (who often dismiss supernatural talk) and at risk with vaesen who might see them as meddlers. In summary, Vaesen provides ghostly tales and eerie adventures steeped in folklore. Sessions will have players quietly exploring misty forests, speaking to frightened or skeptical villagers, uncovering tragic backstories of both people and vaesen, and deciding how to resolve situations that might not have a clear-cut right answer - all while trying to survive the claws of a huldra or the hex of a vengeful vättar long enough to bring about a dawn where humans and hidden folk can coexist in peace, at least for a time.

name: Vast Grimm
description: Vast Grimm is a standalone RPG that mashes up the ultra-light, ultra-deadly style of Mörk Borg with a cosmic horror, science fiction setting. It's essentially a third-party hack on Mörk Borg, which means it has similar rules (d20 rolls, minimal stats, a focus on random tables and emergent storytelling) and a very similar aesthetic of DIY punk art and dark humor, but instead of a fantasy dying world, it's a foul, crumbling universe consumed by a horrific plague. In Vast Grimm, the universe is overrun by the Vast Grimm, an eldritch parasitic infection that corrupts life and technology. The tone is gleefully grimy and nihilistic: expect space hulks full of pulsating flesh growths and half-mad survivors, void-crazed cultists, and a general heavy metal vibe in spaaaaace. Characters are typically mercenaries, survivors, or scoundrels aboard a spaceship, trying to outlive the inevitable end. They have classes like different “Origins” or “Nano classes” (perhaps cybernetic ghoul, vat-grown experiment, etc.), giving a few starting abilities or gear. But like Mörk Borg, characters are disposable and not “balanced” – one might start with an autorifle and another with just a bone knife. The mechanical framework: abilities like Agility, Toughness, etc., which you roll under or add to a d20 roll to beat a difficulty or an opponent's stat. Attacks often roll d20 + relevant mod vs. a target's Defense. Damage might be a flat number or small dice like d6, and there's no leveling in the traditional sense. Instead you might find better equipment or cyber augmentations (with risks). One unique thing is how they handle “Nano powers” or tech-spells – likely there are glitchy technological artifacts that function like spells in MB (with possible catastrophic failures if you roll a 1 or such). The game definitely has a Black Void meets Alien meets Warhammer 40K warp-mutants vibe. There's a plague aspect: possibly PCs themselves could carry infection (maybe tracking an Infection stat), which grants mutation powers at the cost of slowly turning into a Vast Grimm monster. Over time characters will likely lose limbs, gain tentacles, or suffer mind-shattering revelations as results on tables when they push their luck or touch strange objects. The starship part is more backdrop than crunchy 36 spaceship combat; it gives mobility to explore derelict stations or to escape a planet overrun by worm-riddled zombies. Sometimes the ship might itself be falling apart and haunted by the horrors of the cosmos. Vast Grimm's adventures are often scenario-based: maybe answering a distress call on a gore-strewn research facility, or infiltrating a cult stronghold on a shattered moon to steal a device, etc. The game's content encourages creative problem-solving and heavy metal mayhem over tactical planning. Like Mörk Borg, it's about that final blaze of glory. You know doom is coming (in Mörk Borg there's a countdown of world-ending events; in Vast Grimm likely the spread of the plague or cosmic entropic end is inevitable), but you go out guns blazing, one-liners spouting, and possibly chainsawing your way through mutated grotesqueries. In summary: Vast Grimm is a rules-light, attitude-heavy sci-fi horror RPG where you'll roll a handful of dice, consult wild tables for outcomes, and probably laugh at the over-the-top gore and futility of it all even as your last surviving character triggers the reactor overload to wipe out the breeding pit of the Vast Grimm before limping to the escape pod with one arm and an eye left. It's not about winning – it's about dying spectacularly in the grim darkness of the far future, with style." Warhammer 40,000: Imperium Maledictum,TTRPG,"Warhammer 40,000: Imperium Maledictum is a tabletop RPG set in the grim darkness of the far future of Warhammer 40k, focused on the human perspective within the labyrinthine bureaucracy and tyranny of the Imperium of Man. Unlike the older Dark Heresy game where characters are Acolytes of an Inquisitor, Imperium Maledictum positions the players as agents working for a powerful Patron (who could be an Inquisitor, a planetary governor, a high-ranking priest, a Rogue Trader, etc.) undertaking missions in the Patron's interests. This patronage system gives the GM a way to feed the party objectives and also limits them - they have some backing and authority from their patron but also are restricted by their patron's goals and quirks. Characters are often normal (if exceptional) humans (or maybe baseline abhumans like a Voidborn or Hive Worlder, depending on options) rather than transhuman Space Marines or the like. They come from various backgrounds and careers within Imperial society, like Arbitrator (judge/ cop), Chirurgeon (medicae), sanctioned Psyker (with perilous psychic powers), Assassin, Tech-priest of the Adeptus Mechanicus, Cleric of the Ecclesiarchy, Guardsman veteran, or even an Adept (bureaucrat/scribe).

name: Warhammer Fantasy Roleplay
description: Warhammer Fantasy Roleplay (WFRP) is a grim and perilous RPG set in the Old World, the dark fantasy setting of Warhammer Fantasy. It is renowned for mixing low-fantasy adventuring (often starting as lowly peasants or tradesmen) with a richly realized world of corruption, intrigue, and horror. The game lets players experience the Warhammer world from the perspective of everyday people who, through fate or bad luck, get caught up in dangerous plots - fighting Skaven in the sewers beneath a city, uncovering Chaos cults in a village, or surviving the night in a haunted coaching inn, for example. WFRP uses a percentile (d100) system: characters have characteristics (Weapon Skill, Ballistic Skill, Strength, Toughness, Initiative, etc.) and to succeed on a test you generally roll d100 and try to get equal or under your relevant percentage after modifiers. The career system is a hallmark: rather than fixed classes, characters have careers (like Rat Catcher, Soldier, Apothecary, Witch Hunter, etc.) which provide stat advances and skills/talents. You typically start in a basic career (often pretty mundane: Servant, Tradesman, Mercenary, etc.) and can, with experience points, either advance within it or switch to a related career. This gives a sense that characters hold “jobs” in the world and progress organically (the farmhand might become a watchman then a sheriff, etc.). Combat is dangerous: wounds are limited, and while armor and 38 Toughness can absorb some damage, a lucky hit can maim or kill. There's also a critical hit system: dropping to 0 wounds means further hits cause critical injury tables - ranging from minor scars to losing limbs or outright death. Also, disease and poison are prevalent threats; a bite from a giant rat might give you the lethal “Black Plague” over days if untreated. Magic exists but is double-edged: spellcasters (only a few careers like Wizards or Priest of a god in later career tiers) can wield powerful spells, but miscasts can cause disastrous or chaotic effects (summoning a demon accidentally, or your limbs turning to tentacles briefly, etc.), not to mention in many places witches are burned at the stake if discovered. Corruption by Chaos is a theme: encountering horrid monsters or dark sorcery can force Willpower tests to avoid mental trauma or corruption points, which might eventually give mutations (which are illegal and cause many adventurers to hide or amputate them to avoid execution). In terms of tone, Warhammer is famous for its gallows humor and cynicism. The world is sometimes called "grimdark": life is hard, injustices are rife (the peasants are taxed heavily by nobles, roads teem with bandits, the Inquisition might torture innocents in their zeal), and Chaos lurks everywhere ready to exploit human folly. Yet, it's not utterly hopeless - players can be heroes who save villages or thwart cults (though often without recognition or thanks, just a few coins and maybe a recurring nightmare). The Enemy Within campaign (the classic 1st edition epic) is a great example: it starts with a simple misunderstanding on a coach and leads to uncovering a conspiracy that could shake the Empire, all while navigating personal ambition, trust, and temptation. Mechanically and narratively, the game encourages investigation, roleplay, and problem-solving often over hack-and-slash. Many scenarios have you attend a masquerade ball to catch a cult leader, or interrogate suspects after a Chaos artifact theft, or navigate the politics of a town council to secure help, etc. But when combat happens, it's memorable and visceral (you might be terrified of a lone Chaos Warrior because he's likely to disembowel one of you in a single swing). WFRP's world (the Old World, especially the Empire which is like Renaissance Germany with fantasy elements) is richly detailed with conflict not just vs Chaos and monsters but between human factions (religious schisms, noble family feuds, trade guild rivalries). It's a bit like playing in a Renaissance horror story where the protagonists are a bit out of their depth. To summarize, Warhammer Fantasy Roleplay is about adventurers making their way through a cruel and dark world, often just trying to survive or earn some coin, but stumbling onto evils great and small. With a combination of dark humor, deadly combat, and the constant lure of corruption (be it greed, Chaos, or just despair), it creates a gritty and immersive fantasy experience quite distinct from high-heroism games. You might start as a nobody, and even if you become somebody, you'll have the scars (and missing fingers, and recurring plague cough, and occasional nightmares) to show for it.

name: Werewolf: The Apocalypse
description: Werewolf: The Apocalypse is a modern horror- fantasy RPG set in the World of Darkness (the same universe as Vampire: The Masquerade) where players are Garou - werewolves born of three breeding types (homid: human-born, lupus: wolf-born, metis: werewolf-born sterile outcasts) and belonging to one of various tribes (each with a distinct culture and philosophy, like the noble Silver Fangs, the eco-warrior Red Talons, the mystical 39 Stargazers, etc.). The Garou are not cursed individuals like movie werewolves; they are an entire society/culture with a purpose: they believe they were created to be Gaia the Earth Mother's warriors, fighting the Wyrm (a cosmic force of corruption and destruction) and its influence in the world. Werewolf deals with themes of rage, savagery vs. nobility, environmentalism (the Apocalypse often refers to ecological collapse), and the tragedy of being a warrior who will probably die young in an unwinnable war. The system is the Storyteller System (at least in older editions): dice pools of d10s equal to Attribute + Ability, looking for results over a difficulty (often 6), with number of successes determining degree. The twist for Werewolf is the Rage and Gnosis mechanics. Rage is the feral anger inside a Garou (they are volatile); high Rage lets a werewolf do extra actions or recover from stun, but also risk entering frenzy (where the wolf takes over, possibly attacking allies or violating the Veil of secrecy). Gnosis is spiritual connection to Gaia and the spirit world (the Umbra); it's used to activate certain gifts (their special powers) or step sideways into the spirit world. Willpower is also key to resist frenzy or temptations. Garou can shapeshift into five forms, from human to the giant Crinos war-wolf (think classic werewolf form) to full wolf, etc. Combat in Crinos is deadly: werewolves have super strength and can rend normal foes easily, plus they regenerate most damage except silver or very large trauma. But their enemies (like Black Spiral Dancers, Fomori demons, or corporate mercenaries with silver bullets) can still challenge or kill them, especially in number. The vibe of gameplay can oscillate between moments of pure empowerment (few things are as badass as tearing through a Pentex lab full of toxin-spewing zombies as a seven-foot killing machine) and moments of horror/despair (discovering that despite that victory, the river is still polluted and the corrupt oil company is just going to try again somewhere else; also you maybe accidentally killed an innocent during frenzy). The structure often involves packs (the PC group is a pack bound by a totem spirit) going on missions or quests given by elders or demanded by circumstance. This could be in the city (e.g., find and destroy a Wyrm-corrupted drug operation) or in the wilderness (stop loggers from razing a sacred forest) or full Umbra spirit quests (enter the spirit world to gain a powerful ally or learn a ritual). A lot of roleplay comes from Garou society and tribal politics: there are 13 tribes plus the Black Spirals (fallen werewolves to the Wyrm). Tribes have different goals and methods; e.g., the Glass Walkers are city werewolves who use technology - other werewolves see that as taint. Red Talons are mostly lupine and hate humanity (they've even murdered humans to curb their spread), which is awkward in a mixed pack with human-born. There's also interaction with other shapechangers (Garou call them Fera: werecats (Bastet), wereravens (Corax), etc.), who in the lore mostly died out or keep distance after past conflicts. And they have the Litany (their code of laws) which includes things like “combat the Wyrm wherever it dwells,” “respect the territory of another,” “never mate with another Garou” (to avoid producing metis), and these cause moral dilemmas and social trial scenes when broken. The Apocalypse in the title is not just theoretical: canonically, it's close. Many elders think this is the final generation of Garou and the Wyrm will either be defeated in a final stand or Gaia will die. That gives a heavy weight to even small victories: every battle could be your last, and there's a 40 drive to make it count, to die gloriously if needed. But also anger at the state of the world: humans keep making the Wyrm stronger by destroying nature and embracing hate/greed. That anger is a fuel (Rage) but also the curse (frenzy). Mechanically, when you frenzy, the GM can take over and you might kill someone you love or reveal werewolves to onlookers (bad for the Veil/Masquerade). It's the ultimate loss of control in what is partly a game about control vs. letting the beast loose. So, in summary, Werewolf: The Apocalypse lets you play a monster who is also arguably a hero-a savage, blood-soaked hero fighting a losing war to save the world.
